RLock

Another class used for thread synchronization is RLock , also known as the reentrant
lock . This class is very similar to the Lock class, but it can be acquired multiple times
by the same thread. Inside it, in addition to the locked-unlocked state , there exists
information on the owner thread and on the recursion level.
```
Like a Lock , an RLock can be acquired from a thread using the acquire()
```

method. At this point RLock becomes locked , and the calling thread becomes one of the
owners. Similarly, an RLock can be unlocked by calling the release() method.
This time, however, unlike the Lock synchronization mechanism, the calls to the acquire()
and release() methods can be nested. This means that the same thread may acquire the
RLock several times before releasing it. However, the number of release() calls must
exactly match the number of acquire() calls made by that thread. If a thread acquires an
RLock three times, it must also release it three times. Otherwise, the lock will never be fully
released and will result in a deadlock. Other threads that will invoke the acquire()
method will be added to the list of owners. Only the last matching release() call from the
owning thread will fully unlock the RLock, while allowing another thread that is waiting
on acquire() to proceed. Intermediate release() calls just decrease the recursion depth,
but they keep the lock reserved for the same thread. Importantly, only the thread that
acquired the lock can release it—other threads cannot call release() on its behalf.
```
In the following example, each thread executes a function that runs three outer itera-
```

tions. In each iteration, the thread acquires the lock once at the outer level, and two times
more inside a nested loop. At each inner loop step, it increments the shared variable by 1.
After completing the nested loop, it increments the shared variable one more time before
releasing the lock. As a result, each outer iteration increases the shared value by (2 from
the inner loop + 1 from the outer loop) = 3 increments . Since there are three outer
iterations, each thread contributes a total of 9 increments . With three threads running,
the expected final value of the shared variable is 27 . This expected outcome helps
the reader understand how the RLock ensures consistent, and predictable updates despite
concurrent execution.
```
import threading
import time
shared = 0
rlock = threading.RLock()
def func(name, t):
```

```
local = shared
time.sleep(t)

rlock.acquire()
local += 1
time.sleep(2)
shared = local
print("Thread %s-%s wrote: %s" %(name, j, shared))
rlock.release()
shared = local + 1
print("Thread %s wrote: %s" %(name, shared))
rlock.release()

t2 = threading.Thread(target = func,args=('B',10,))
```

Semaphore

Another synchronization mechanism available in the threading module is the semaphore
, one of the oldest primitives in the history of computer science, which was introduced by
Edsger W. Dijkstra in the 1960s. The main purpose of a semaphore is to regulate concurrent access to a finite set of resources. Conceptually, a semaphore behaves like a counter:
each call to acquire() decreases its value by one, while each call to release() increases it
again. As long as the counter remains greater than or equal to zero, a thread that calls
acquire() is allowed to proceed. If, however, the counter has reached zero, the thread is
blocked and must wait until another thread releases the semaphore, thus freeing up one “
slot ” for access.
```
It is important to distinguish the semaphore from the simpler lock. A lock can be seen
```

as a particular case of semaphore, which is initialized with a counter equal to one. In
this situation, only a single thread at a time can enter the protected section, while enforcing
strict mutual exclusion. A semaphore, on the other hand, can be initialized with any
integer value, allowing up to that number of threads to simultaneously access the resource.
This makes it more flexible and suitable in scenarios where resources are limited but can
be shared by more than one thread at once—for example, a pool of database connections, a
set of network sockets, or even a limited number of printers in a system.
```
When a thread calls acquire() it must eventually call release() once it has finished with
```

the shared resource; otherwise other threads will remain blocked and the program may
encounter a deadlock. Figure 2.2 sketches the classic producer–consumer pattern: a
producer thread generates data and places it into shared memory, while a consumer thread
removes and processes that data. The two run at different and variable speeds, and
there may be multiple producers or consumers. This makes the pattern a natural fit for
concurrency.
```
Figure 2.2: The Producer-Consumer Model
To coordinate the handoff correctly with semaphores we will model a single-slot buffer
```

. We use two counting semaphores: one (slots) tracks whether the slot is available, and
the other (items) tracks whether a produced item is ready to be consumed. The producer
waits on slots, writes the value, and then signals items; the consumer waits on items, reads
the value, and then signals slots. This scheme guarantees that the consumer never reads
before the producer has written, and that the producer never overwrites an unread value.
With this in mind, let us implement the example in the following code:
```
import threading

```

```
This implementation uses two semaphores—slots (initialized to 1) and items (initialized
```

to 0)—to enforce correct handoff on a single-slot buffer. The producer must acquire a free
slot before writing and then releases an available item; the consumer waits for an available
item, reads it, and then releases the slot. The print_lock exists only to keep the
output lines neat. By executing the code just written, we will get the following:
```
producer -> put 4 (item 1)
consumer <- got 4 (item 1)
producer -> put 65 (item 2)

consumer <- got 92 (item 3)

consumer <- got 5 (item 5)

As we can see, the producer and consumer are alternating perfectly. Each value pro-
```

duced is immediately consumed, and no items are skipped or overwritten. This happens
because we are now using two semaphores to model the two aspects of the problem: the
number of free slots in the buffer and the number of available items. The slots semaphore
ensures that the producer cannot add more items than the buffer can hold, while the items
semaphore guarantees that the consumer waits until there is something to consume. In
this way, production and consumption remain synchronized, avoiding the race conditions
and data losses we observed in the earlier examples.
```
This pattern is a canonical use of semaphores: they are not only used for mutual ex-
```

clusion like locks, but also for coordinating access to limited resources between multiple
threads.
```
In conclusion, semaphores are a powerful tool but require careful design. They are not
```

a universal replacement for locks in critical sections—instead, they provide more flexible
control over how many threads can simultaneously access a resource. In our single-buffer
example, the combined use of semaphores for “ free slots ” and “ready items” ensures that
the producer does not overwrite data that has not yet been consumed and that the consumer

<a id='p184'></a>
<!-- Página 184 -->

184 SEMAPHORE

does not wait unnecessarily. This scheme eliminates the race conditions we observed in
the less protected versions.
```
However, it is important to be aware of their limitations: semaphores can introduce
```

overhead (in terms of acquire/release operations), they may lead to starvation of certain
threads if not managed fairly, and they can complicate program logic when many resources
or many threads are involved. Moreover, because semaphores allow multiple threads to
enter simultaneously (up to the configured limit), they do not enforce the total exclusion that
a Lock provides. This can be perfectly acceptable when the resource allows concurrent
use, but insufficient when strict consistency is required, especially with complex shared
data structures.
```
Finally, when designing concurrent programs, it is always essential to define clearly what
```

the “ atomic unit ” of work should be, to check whether the resource is truly shared,
whether the number of accessing threads needs to be limited, and that every acquire()
is always paired with a release() , even in the case of exceptions. Using semaphores
within a with statement (when supported as a context manager) or by placing the corresponding release() call in a finally block ensures that the semaphore is
always released, even if an exception occurs, thereby improving both reliability and code
readability.
```
With these precautions in mind, semaphores can become a valuable synchronization
```

tool that strike a balance between performance, safety, and controlled parallelism.

<!-- Página 185 -->

Condition

An alternative synchronization primitive provided by the threading module is the Condition
class. Unlike a simple Lock or Semaphore, which only regulates access to resources, a
Condition is designed for situations where threads must wait for a particular state of
shared data before continuing.
A Condition is always associated with a lock to ensure that checks and updates to the
shared state happen atomically. Beyond the usual acquire() and release() operations, it
provides three key methods:

• wait() , which releases the lock and suspends the thread until it is notified.
• notify() , which wakes up one waiting thread.
• notify_all() , which wakes up all waiting threads.

```
This makes conditions especially useful for coordination patterns like the producer–
```

consumer model, where a consumer should not proceed until data has been produced and a
producer should wait until the previous data has been consumed. In such cases, Condition
allows threads to signal each other explicitly, which ensures that work is carried out in the
right order without busy waiting or resource overwriting.
```
To illustrate, we can rewrite our earlier producer–consumer example so that the pro-
```

ducer signals the consumer when new data is available and the consumer signals the producer when it has finished using the data. The result is a clean alternation between the
two threads as is shown here:
```

import time, random
condition = Condition()
shared = None # buffer starts empty
count = 5 # number of items to produce/consume
class Consumer(Thread):
def __init__(self, count):
super().__init__()
self.count = count
def run(self):
global shared
for _ in range(self.count):
```

```
with condition:
while shared is None:
condition.wait() # wait until producer provides data
print(f"consumer <- got {shared}")
shared = None
condition.notify() # signal producer to produce next item
class Producer(Thread):
def __init__(self, count):
super().__init__()
self.count = count
def run(self):
global shared
for i in range(self.count):
time.sleep(1)
item = random.randint(0, 100)
with condition:
while shared is not None:
condition.wait() # wait until consumer has used the item
shared = item
print(f"producer -> put {item}")
condition.notify() # signal consumer that data is ready
t1 = Producer(count)
t2 = Consumer(count)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
In this code, both the producer and the consumer coordinate through the same Condition
```

object. The producer acquires the condition lock, generates a new value, and then calls
notify() to signal the consumer that fresh data is available. The consumer, on the
other hand, waits on the condition whenever the shared resource is not ready. When it is
awakened by the producer’s signal, it consumes the value, resets the shared variable, and
notifies the producer that it can generate the next item.
```
This back-and-forth mechanism ensures that the two threads alternate their work, with-
```

out interfering with each other. Unlike the semaphore-based solution, which only controlled how many threads could enter a critical section, the condition variable explicitly
models the state of the shared resource , and allows threads to wait until that state
changes.
```

```

protocol of interaction between the two threads: the producer waits until the consumer
has consumed the last value and the consumer waits until the producer has generated a
new one. This makes conditions particularly useful when threads must coordinate on
an occasion something happens, and not just on how many threads can enter a critical
section.

Event

In addition to the Semaphore and the Condition , there is another synchronization mechanism. It is called Event , which can be understood as a basic
mechanism of communication between threads in which a thread signals a certain event to
another thread waiting for it to happen.
```
An Event object manages an internal Boolean flag. There are also two methods
```

that determine its value. The set() method sets the flag value to True , while the
clear() method to False . False is the default value of the Event object when
it is created. There is also a third method, wait() , which blocks the calling thread
until the flag becomes True. If multiple threads are waiting on the same Event, they will
all be released as soon as another thread calls set() .
```
In other words, a thread, during its execution, freezes by calling the wait() method,
```

while waiting for an event to continue. In another thread, when this event occurs, the
set() method unlocks the previous thread, which performs its operations, and then
calls clear() to reset everything.
```
In our example of the two threads Producer and Consumer , we can replace
```

the previous mechanisms with the Event-based synchronization mechanism.
```
Let us modify the code as follows:
from threading import Thread, Event
import time
import random
event = Event()
shared = 1
count = 5
class Consumer(Thread):
def __init__(self, count):
Thread.__init__(self)
global event
self.count = count
def run(self):
global shared
for i in range(self.count):
event.wait()
print("consumer has used this: %s" %shared)
```

```
return random.randint(0,100)

global shared
for i in range(self.count):
shared = self.request()
print("producer has loaded this: %s" %shared)
event.set()
t1 = Producer(count)
t2 = Consumer(count)
t1.start()
t2.start()
t1.join()
t2.join()
```

In these cases, the Queue comes to our aid.
By modifying the previous code, we remove the shared variable and replace it
with a Queue that will be able to correctly manage the distribution between concurrent threads, whether it is a Producer or a Consumer .
```
from threading import Thread
from queue import Queue
import time
import random
queue = Queue()
shared = 1
count = 5
class Consumer(Thread):
def __init__(self, count):
Thread.__init__(self)
self.count = count
def run(self):
global queue
for i in range(self.count):
local = queue.get()
print("consumer has used this: %s" %local)
queue.task_done()
class Producer(Thread):
def __init__(self, count):
Thread.__init__(self)
self.count = count
def request(self):
time.sleep(1)
return random.randint(0,100)
def run(self):
global queue
for i in range(self.count):
local = self.request()
queue.put(local)
print("producer has loaded this: %s" %local)
t1 = Producer(count)
t2 = Producer(count)
t3 = Consumer(count)
t4 = Consumer(count)
t1.start()
t2.start()
t3.start()
t4.start()
```

## 204 PARALLEL PROGRAMMING WITH PROCESSES


<a id='p205'></a>
<!-- Página 205 -->

Introduction

In this chapter, we will work with parallel programming. In fact, it is only the processes
that can run simultaneously in Python and brings the real benefits of parallel computing.
In Python, there are two main approaches through which processes can be implemented
in parallel programming: the multiprocessing module of the standard library and the
mpi4py library, which extends the MPI protocol for Python. Multiprocessing implements the shared memory programming paradigm, where processes within the program
can access a common memory area. As with threads, this approach would create race
conditions and synchronization problems. To tackle this, we will introduce two communication channels between processes that are provided by the same multiprocessing module:
Queue and Pipe . These will allow parallel processes to exchange data in perfect
synchronization without encountering the problems associated with shared memory. The
mpi4py library, on the other hand, is based on the message passing paradigm. In this
model, there are no shared resources and all communication between processes takes place
via the exchange of processes.




```

```


<a id='p206'></a>
<!-- Página 206 -->

<a id='p207'></a>

• Multiprocessing Module
• Process ID (PID)
• Process as Subclass
• Channels of Communication: Queue and Pipe
• Process Pool
• ProcessPoolExecutor
• Mpi4py Library
• Point-to-point Communication
• Collective Communication
• Topologies

## 208 STRUCTURE

Processes and the Multiprocessing
Module

In Python, the real protagonists of parallel programming are processes. This is because
are the only way to achieve true parallel execution of CPU-bound code. This limitation is
due to the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython, which prevents multiple threads from
executing Python bytecode simultaneously. However, it is important to note that threads
are very effective for I/O-bound tasks ( such as file operations or network communication),
since in these cases the GIL is released during I/O operations, which allows concurrent and
even parallel progress for multiple threads.
Programming processes in Python is very important, so much so that we have a module
completely dedicated to them in the standard library, which is known as multiprocessing
.
This module offers all the possible operations for creating and managing processes within
a program. It is akin to what the threading module does with threads. The instructions
and constructs used in the implementation are almost identical:

• The Process() constructor allows the creation of a process.
• Calling the start() method starts the process activity.
• Calling the join() method causes the main process to wait until the specific
```
process on which it is invoked has completed its execution. Therefore, if multiple
processes have been launched in parallel, join() must be called individually on
each of them (as shown in the exemplar code in this section) to ensure that all processes
are completed before the program continues.

```

The process life cycle is based on three states:

• Ready
• Running
• Waiting

It is only then that the multiprocessing module structures parallel programming. The
main process starts with the execution of the program. Within it, a number of processes
are defined using the Process() constructor. At this point the processes just defined
are in the Ready state. Then at a certain point, the part of the program is started for

```
209
```


<a id='p210'></a>
<!-- Página 210 -->


## 210 PROCESSES AND THE MULTIPROCESSING MODULE





```
Figure 34:


```

execution in parallel. All defined processes (children processes) will be activated together
by calling the start() method for each of them. The main process, in this
case also the parent process, will continue its execution asynchronously, and will not wait
for the execution of the child processes (see Figure 3.1 ):
```
Figure 3.1: Asynchronous Mode Without Join()
```

If instead, we want a synchronization mechanism, and would like the main process to
wait for the result of the child processes, we will call the join() method for each
process as shown in Figure 3.2 :
```
Figure 3.2: Synchronous Mode With Join()
```

Like how we dealt with the threads of the threading module, we write the code with the
processes. As you can see, the API design between threads and processes is consistent.
Each process that is activated in parallel will perform certain operations specified by

different operations. In fact, the target function is specified for every single process
by passing its name as the target argument in the constructor.
```
To better understand these concepts, let us consider following code:
import multiprocessing

print ("start Process %i" %i)
time.sleep(2)
print ("end Process %i" %i)
return
if __name__ == '__main__':
p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=function, args=(1,))
p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=function, args=(2,))
p3 = multiprocessing.Process(target=function, args=(3,))
p4 = multiprocessing.Process(target=function, args=(4,))
p5 = multiprocessing.Process(target=function, args=(5,))
p1.start()
p2.start()
p3.start()
p4.start()
p5.start()
p1.join()
p2.join()
p3.join()
p4.join()
p5.join()
print("END Program")
As we can see in the code, five processes are defined in parallel through the Process()
```

constructor. They will all perform the same target function. If the function needs some
arguments here, you can also pass them to the Process() constructor as a tuple
to the args argument. In the code, we will pass a number that we need to identify
the process running within the function. All these processes will be activated with the
start() method and then synchronized with the main processes through the join()
method.
```

The way to implement the code in parallel as we did in the previous case is very readable
```

as all the instructions are expressed individually and explicitly. Since we have to use five
processes in parallel, we have defined five lines for the constructors, five lines to activate
them with the start method, and five lines to synchronize them with the main process with
the join() method. However, if the number of processes was more than in this
code, implementing them could have been very problematic.

mechanisms to generalize all the previous steps. An example of modifying the preceding

Using Process IDs

In the previous case, we used the passage of the arguments within the Process()
constructor to communicate the process number through the iterator i . There is
another way to identify running processes among themselves, by means of their Process
ID ( PID ). It is a very simple operation, we import the os module of the standard
library that provides us with the getpid() function. The latter allows us to obtain
the PID of each running process.
```
We apply the following changes to the previous code, replacing the numbers with the
```

process ID, as follows:
```
import multiprocessing
import os
import time
def function():
pid = os.getpid()
print ("start Process %s" %pid)
time.sleep(2)
print ("end Process %s" %pid)
return
if __name__ == '__main__':
processes = []
n_procs = 5
for I in range(n_procs):
p = multiprocessing.Process(target=function)
processes.append(p)
p.start()
for i in range(n_procs):
processes[i].join()
print("END Program")
You can see that the Process() constructor no longer needs to use args
```

as an argument, as the function itself will handle it. Inside it, there is the call to the
getpid() function that will return the PID of the process in which it will be executed.
We will get five different PIDs from the same function, without having to use arguments
passed from the main process.
```
If we run the code, we will obtain the following result:
```

Process Pool

A further evolution of the programming pattern to manage multiple processes together is
to use a process pool , which is expressed in Python by multiprocessing.Pool
class.
```
A pool is that object responsible for a certain number of processes. Through it you
```

will have control of their status, from creation to use, and whether or not some of them
should be paused to save computational resources. multiprocessing.Pool is an
interface for the ad hoc execution of a specific task, while making use of a set of processes,
without having to specify how many and which processes will have to perform this task.
This allows us to simplify the code and make it more readable.
```
Let us take the previous code, and convert it this time using multiprocessing.Pool
```

:
```
import multiprocessing
import time
def function(i):
process = multiprocessing.current_process()
print ("start Process %i(pid:%s)" %(i,process.pid))
time.sleep(2)
print ("end Process %i(pid:%s)" %(i,process.pid))
return
if __name__ == '__main__':
pool = multiprocessing.Pool()
print("Processes started: %s" %pool._processes)
for i in range(pool._processes):
results = pool.apply(function, args=(i,))
pool.close()
print("END Program")
There are many changes within the code that we need to account for. First, we used
```

the constructor of the class to define a process pool:
```
pool = multiprocessing.pool.Pool()
This will create a process pool that will use a number of worker processes that match
```

the number of logical CPU cores in your system. This number is accessible in code via
pool._processes . Then pool.apply() is used to make the pool execute a
given task represented by the function() function, while passing it the number of


<!-- Página 218 -->

218 PROCESS POOL

the process generated via args as an argument. Once all the tasks required in the
code have been performed, the pool will be closed using the pool.close() function.
```
As for the function() function, we have added the PID of the process, so that
```

it can be recognized unambiguously. To obtain this value, first, the running process is
obtained with current_process() and then the pid attribute is invoked on
this.

Define Processes as Subclasses

So far, we have seen how to define in code the processes that will work in parallel via the
Process() constructor. This was then assigned a target function containing the code
to execute in parallel . Another way to implement the scheme of processes in parallel
is to define the latter as subclasses of Process() . Within these, their functionality
will then be specified by overriding the __init __() and run() methods.
In this case, the code to run in parallel will be inserted into the run() method of the
class.
```
Let us get a better understanding of this concept in a practical way, taking the following
```

```
import random

time.sleep(2)
print ("end Process %s" %self.count)
if __name__ == '__main__':
processes = []
n_procs = 5
for i in range(n_procs):
p = ChildProcess(i)
processes.append(p)
p.start()
for i in range(n_procs):
processes[i].join()
As we can see from the code, we define a subclass of Process() which we have
```

called ChildProcess() . Within the class, we have two overridden methods. In
__init __() , we will define the attributes of the subclass to be added, as in this case,

Channels of Communication between
Processes

Processes, unlike threads , generally do not share a memory space, and therefore need a
different mechanism to be able to communicate with each other and exchange data. The
multiprocessing module, however, is based on a shared memory paradigm , and allows
users to share resources between processes. Since this practice leads to the same problems we encountered, while dealing with threads with race condition phenomena and lack
of synchronization between processes, it is not recommended to use it. The multiprocessing module provides like the threading module the same tools for process synchronization,
such as semaphores , locks , events , and so on, but it is not recommended to follow
this approach. Unlike threads, to work with a set of processes in parallel, the multiprocessing module provides communication channels to be used as secure and synchronized
data exchange mechanisms. There are two different modes of communication channels:

• Queues
• Pipes

These channels are defined within the code through the Queue and Pipe classes
provided by the multiprocessing module. Both are equipped with Queue() and
Pipe() constructors, and a whole series of methods that manage the exchange of data
between processes and their internal synchronization mechanisms. These communication
channels, once defined at the main process level, are excellent tools for exchanging data in a
perfectly synchronized manner. In fact, thanks to them, the processes will be able to send
and receive data in a safe and synchronized way, without the risk of race conditions.
Furthermore, if the data sent is more than requested, these will not be overwritten, but
accumulated within these objects, and provide for the buffering of data.




```
223
```


<a id='p224'></a>
<!-- Página 224 -->


## 224 CHANNELS OF COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PROCESSES


<a id='p225'></a>
<!-- Página 225 -->

The Queues

The Queues that we will use as a communication channel between the processes are
implemented by the multiprocessing module. In Python, there are queues belonging to
the queue module (which we have already used with threads). But in reality, the internal
implementations are different and multiprocessing.Queue uses a different data
transfer mechanism which is specific to working with processes. In other words, they use
the message passing paradigm exclusively for processes, and avoid using synchronization
mechanisms to add to the queues.
```
Queue is a data structure that implements a First IN-First OUT ( FIFO ) queue.
```

Processes will be able to add data to the queue through the put() method or receive
data from it through the get() method. The order of the data entered is maintained
within the queue and the data sent to the processes that request them will then follow the
order of entry.
```
The data can be accumulated within the queue, which can store both simple numerical
```

values and complex objects. By default, the Queue() constructor sets maxsize=0
, which means the queue has no logical size limit. However, the actual capacity is still
constrained by the system’s available memory. If you wish, you can specify a capacity
limit by passing a positive integer to the maxsize parameter, which represents the
maximum number of objects the queue can contain.
```
queue = multiprocessing.Queue(maxsize=100)
In the context of the capacity of a queue, it is important to know the current number of
```

objects contained within it during execution. For this purpose, there is a qsize()
method which returns this number:
```
size = queue.qsize()
Still, in the context of managing a queue when you want to affix conditions to the pro-
```

gram flow, it might be useful to know if a queue is empty or full. The empty()
method returns a Boolean that has the value True when the queue is empty , while the
full() method returns True if the queue is full. This is demonstrated as follows:
```
if queue.empty():
…
if queue.full():
…
In order to better understand how a queue works, we can use the consumer-producer
```

paradigm , which is useful while sending and receiving data. The producer can be

```
225
```


<a id='p226'></a>
<!-- Página 226 -->

226

any process that will provide data after its execution and the consumer can be any process
that will need that data in order to complete its execution. To make this mechanism work,
which is created by at least two processes, an exchange of data will be necessary. Since
the processes do not have a common memory area, they will exchange their data through
the queue. The consumer will send the produced data to the queue, while the consumer
will request them from the producer . Consumers and producers are always
asynchronous as they usually do not depend except for the data flow that happens via the
queue. Since the times of the consumer and producer rarely coincide, there may be cases
in which the producer produces consumer data faster, and these can be accumulated
in an orderly manner within the queue, without being overwritten. The consumer will
thus have plenty of time to use this produced data in an orderly manner.
```
The following code implements a simple producer-consumer paradigm which is based
```

on two parallel processes that use a queue to exchange data:
```
from multiprocessing import Process, Queue
import time
import random
class Consumer(Process):
def __init__(self, count, queue):
Process.__init__(self)
self.count = count
self.queue = queue
def run(self):
for i in range(self.count):
local = self.queue.get()
time.sleep(2)
print("consumer has used this: %s" %local)
class Producer(Process):
def __init__(self, count, queue):
Process.__init__(self)
self.count = count
self.queue = queue
def request(self):
time.sleep(1)
return random.randint(0,100)
def run(self):
for i in range(self.count):
local = self.request()
self.queue.put(local)
print("producer has loaded this: %s" %local)
if __name__ == '__main__':
queue = Queue()
count = 5
```


<a id='p227'></a>
<!-- Página 227 -->

```
227

p1 = Producer(count, queue)
p2 = Consumer(count, queue)
p1.start()
p2.start()
p1.join()
p2.join()
```

Running the code will produce the following result:
```

producer has loaded this: 30
consumer has used this: 55
producer has loaded this: 60
producer has loaded this: 14
consumer has used this: 30
producer has loaded this: 97
consumer has used this: 60
consumer has used this: 14
consumer has used this: 97
```

As we can see, the values generated by the producer process are accumulated within the
queue and subsequently used by the consumer process in perfect synchrony, without losing
or overwriting of values.

Pipes

The other class that performs the functions of the communication channel between processes is the Pipe . The pipe implements two-way communication between
the two processes and is designed to send and receive data between them. Like the
queue class, it has its own Pipe() constructor which will create two different
multiprocessing.connection.Connection objects when it is declared. So, when
you declare the Pipe() constructor, you put the two instances of the connections
separately:
```
conn1, conn2 = multiprocessing.Pipe()
With duplex=True (the default), both ends of the pipe are full-duplex; each
```

connection can be used to both send and receive data. In practice, it is often convenient
to adopt a convention (for example, using one end primarily for sending and the other for
receiving), but this is not enforced by Python.
```
In addition to the bidirectional mode , a pipe can also be created in duplex mode , in
```

which each of the two connections can be used to both send and receive data. In this case,
we will have to set the duplex argument passed in the constructor to True :
```
conn1, conn2 = multiprocessing.Pipe(duplex=True)
In both modes, the processes, through the two generated Connection objects, will be
```

able to send data through the send() method and receive them through the recv()
method:
```
conn2.send(object)
object = conn1.recv()
As for the queues, there is no limit to the size of the objects to be sent; the only condition
```

is that they are pickable . When sent, they will be picked, and then upon being received,
they will automatically be unpicked.
```
As with the Queue, the Pipe class also provides a set of methods that manage the
```

connections that were created for their use. For example, the state of the pipe can be
controlled by the poll() function. This function returns a Boolean: True if there
is data in the connection waiting to be received by a process. This method is very useful
in conditions to manage the flow of execution of a program and is shown as follows:
```
if conn1.poll():
Let us see the concepts just exposed through an example code, like the following one:
from multiprocessing import Process, Pipe
import time

229
```

230 PIPES

```
import random
class Consumer(Process):
def __init__(self, count, conn):
Process.__init__(self)
self.count = count
self.conn = conn
def run(self):
for i in range(self.count):
local = self.conn.recv()
time.sleep(2)
print("consumer has used this: %s" %local)
class Producer(Process):
def __init__(self, count, conn):
Process.__init__(self)
self.count = count
self.conn = conn
def request(self):
time.sleep(1)
return random.randint(0,100)
def run(self):
for i in range(self.count):
local = self.request()
self.conn.send(local)
print("producer has loaded this: %s" %local)
if __name__ == '__main__':
recver, sender = Pipe()
count = 5
p1 = Producer(count, sender)
p2 = Consumer(count, recver)
p1.start()
p2.start()
p1.join()
p2.join()
recver.close()
sender.close()
```

Also, in this case, we used the producer-consumer paradigm, and retained the code
used with the queue previously. This is to help the reader make appropriate comparisons
between the two modes. After running the code, you will get the following result:
```
producer has loaded this: 0
producer has loaded this: 76
consumer has used this: 0
producer has loaded this: 28
```

```
consumer has used this: 76
producer has loaded this: 75
consumer has used this: 28
consumer has used this: 90
consumer has used this: 75
```

At the end of using the pipe, we called the close() method for each of the two
connections. This operation is important to release all the resources used by the pipe.
The most important, and perhaps, the most limiting aspect of pipes is that they work
exclusively between two endpoints, and therefore between only two processes. If you
have to work with several processes at the same time, you will need to establish a pipe for
each pair. It is clear that when there are several processes that work in parallel, managing
pipes will become problematic .

Pipe versus Queue

We have just seen that as communication channels, the multiprocessing module provides
both pipes and queues as a solution. So, which of the two should we choose to exchange
data between processes in parallel?
```
At the first glance, given the limited use of Pipes between only two processes, it would
```

seem that a queue is always the best solution. But that is not necessarily true .
```
Pipe is a much simpler class than a queue. They are implemented at a low level and
```

it is this feature that makes them more efficient and potentially faster for exchanging data
between two processes. Therefore, if this type of connection can be used between pairs
of processes, it is preferable to a queue. If, on the other hand, the data exchange is
consistent and the number of processes involved in this exchange is large, queue is the
more appropriate option.





Mapping of a Function through a
Process Pool

Another important aspect of parallel programming is the mapping of a function. In fact, it
is possible to extend the functionality of map() in Python between multiple processes
in parallel. This function is useful when you want to apply a function on an iterable
object. The map() function applies the function to each element of the object and
returns an array of elements of equal size , where each bears the result of the function.
```
To better understand how the map() function works, consider the following code:
import time
import math
import numpy as np
def func(value):
result = math.sqrt(value)
print("The value %s and the elaboration is %s" %(value, result) )
return result
if __name__ == '__main__':
data = np.array([10,3,6,1])
results = map(func, data)
for result in results:
print("This is the result: %s" %result)
In the code, we have chosen a NumPy array of four elements on which we will apply
```

the function func() . As a result, we will get an array of four elements, each with
the return value of the function applied to the corresponding element.
```
After running the code, we will obtain the following:
The value 10 and the elaboration is 3.1622776601683795
This is the result: 3.1622776601683795
The value 3 and the elaboration is 1.7320508075688772
This is the result: 1.7320508075688772
The value 6 and the elaboration is 2.449489742783178
This is the result: 2.449489742783178
The value 1 and the elaboration is 1.0
This is the result: 1.0

```


<a id='p236'></a>
<!-- Página 236 -->


## 236 MAPPING OF A FUNCTION THROUGH A PROCESS POOL


```
This iterable object mapping mechanism can be extended in parallel program-
```

ming. The efficiency can grow enormously if the calculation of the function on each
element takes place in parallel. For example, each element can be assigned to a process
whose target is just the function passed in map() . In this case, all elements would
be calculated at the same time. For an array of n elements, a normal program would
take n * t time, where t is the execution time of the function. In the parallel case, the
same array of n elements would be passed to n processes, and the execution time would
be limited to t (if there are n cores or n processors in the system). Therefore, the
increase in efficiency is clear.
```
For parallel mapping of a function, the multiprocessing module provides the multiprocessing.poo
```

class. This class provides two methods for this:

• map()
• map_async()

```
In the case of parallel programming, there are two methods that exist because of the
```

different synchronizations that are possible. They both work similarly, except that the
map() function should be used when we need to block program execution until all
target functions in parallel have completed their work. The map_async() function
should be used when it does not block the entire execution of the program.
```
The map() method receives two arguments, the target function, and the
```

iterable object, which is as follows:
```
results = pool.map(target, iterable):
As the name implies, the pool class will create a pool of processes equal to the
```

number of elements of the iterable and will pass the target function to
these processes.
```
However, to better understand these concepts and how they work, it is necessary to move
```

on to practical examples like this code here:
```
import time
import math
import numpy as np
from multiprocessing.pool import Pool
def func(value):
result = math.sqrt(value)
print("The value %s and the elaboration is %s" %(value, result) )
time.sleep(value)
return result
if __name__ == '__main__':
with Pool() as pool:
data = np.array([10,3,6,1])
results = pool.map(func, data)
print("The main process is going on…")
```

```
import time
import math
import numpy as np
from multiprocessing.pool import Pool
def func(value):
result = math.sqrt(value)
print("The value %s and the elaboration is %s" %(value, result) )
time.sleep(value)
return result
if __name__ == '__main__':
with Pool() as pool:
data = np.array([10,3,6,1])
results = pool.map_async(func, data)
print("Main Process is going on…")
for result in results.get():
print("This is the result: %s" %result)
print("END Program")
```

```
As we can see from the two different results, we got the behavior we expected. Using
```

the map() method, you have a synchronization mechanism that interrupts the flow
of execution of the main process. This does not restart until all parallel processes
launched by map() finish their execution. In fact, the text Main process is
going on… appears only after all child processes have finished their task and returned
their results. While using map_async() , the execution of the main process goes on and does not wait for the complete evaluation of results. The text Main
process is going on… appears at the beginning of the text.

Mapping in Parallel with
Chunksize

The map() function will apply a function to each element in an iterable .
If the iterable has a large number of elements, it may be very inefficient to call as
many processes to execute them.
```
A more efficient approach is to divide the elements of the iterable into portions
```

of a certain number of elements, where each is assigned to a process. This can be achieved
by passing the chunksize argument to the map() function.
```
Let us modify the example code we used earlier for the map() method, while in-
```

creasing the number of elements in the np.array() . We will then set portions of
four elements of the array for each process, passing the chunksize argument equal
to 4 to the map() method.
```
import time
import math
import numpy as np
from multiprocessing.pool import Pool
def func(value):
result = math.sqrt(value)
print("The value %s and the elaboration is %s" %(value, result) )
time.sleep(value)
return result
if __name__ == '__main__':
with Pool() as pool:
data = np.array([10,3,6,1,4,5,2,9,7,3,4,6])
results = pool.map(func, data, chunksize=4)
print("The main process is going on…")
for result in results:
print("This is the result: %s" %result)
print("END Program")
This code will generate the following result:
The value 10 and the elaboration is 3.1622776601683795
The value 4 and the elaboration is 2.0
```

The ProcessPoolExecutor

We have a similar mechanism to that of process pools with another class, the ProcessPoolExecutor,
which is distributed by the concurrent.future module. This class also provides
a pool of reusable processes to perform specific operations, including map() .
```
Also, in this case, you will specify the name of the target function to execute and
```

the iterable on which the function will be applied. Once all the assigned tasks
have been completed, the ProcessPoolExecutor must be closed in order to release
all the resources used. The shutdown() function is used for closing.
```
But even in this case, there are simpler and more efficient constructs that can be used.
```

In fact, the ProcessPoolExecutor is compatible with the context manager and the
with declaration as shown here:
```
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
In this case, when execution exits the context manager block, the shutdown()
function is called automatically. The context manager is equivalent to the following:
try:
executor = ProcessPoolExecutor()
finally:
executor.shutdown()
It is therefore clear that the use of a context manager is very convenient in these cases.
```

The ProcessPoolExecutor is thus useful for running the map() function in
parallel . We can see it in the following code:
```

time.sleep(value)
return result
if __name__ == '__main__':
with ProcessPoolExecutor(10) as executor:
data = np.array([10,3,6,1])
for result in executor.map(func, data):
```

The mpi4py Library

A completely different approach to parallel programming in Python using processes is using
the Message Passage Interface ( MPI ). This is a communication protocol which
is standard for parallel programming and is particularly useful in systems with multiple
nodes (multiple processors). This protocol has been implemented in many programming
languages such as Fortran and C.
```
Python also has a number of MPI modules useful for parallel programming. The most
```

interesting of these is the mpi4py library. This was developed based on the MPI-1/2
specification and provides an object-oriented interface based on MPI-2 C ++ bindings .
```
This library is based on general concepts that are very different from those used in the
```

multiprocessing module and with the standard Python library. These concepts are based
on standards developed specifically for multiprocessor and distributed architectures, as
well as clusters. It is therefore clear that the execution methods and the code constructs
are very different from those seen in the first part of the chapter.
```
But, why should one use MPI modules instead of the multiprocessing module? This is
```

due to many factors. The first is because MPI has practically become a standard of parallel
programming for many programming languages, including Python, and is adaptable to the
most varied architectures. At the same time, it can also be used on simple systems with
a single multi-core computer, where the efficiency of the calculation is not so evident.
However, it is useful for practicing and developing programs in parallel and can be adapted
to very complex architectures.
```
First, you need to install the mpi4py library. For Anaconda, run the command:
conda install mpi4py
If you are using Python, you will use pip :
pip install mpi4py
Installing the Python module alone is not enough to work with this library. In order to
```

work, it requires an MPI implementation such as MPICH, Open MPI, or Microsoft-MPI. So,
you will need to download one of these implementations and then install it on your system.
```
For Windows : Download and Install Microsoft MPI (MS-MPI).
For Linux and MacOS : Download MPICH or OpenMPI.
On Ubuntu:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install mpich
On MacOS:

245
```


<a id='p246'></a>
<!-- Página 246 -->

246 THE MPI4PY LIBRARY

```
brew install mpich
```

For the execution of programs in Python, instead of the classic python command,
you will have to use the following wording from the shell:
```
mpiexec -n x python mpi4py _name.py
```

Add mpiexec to your PATH if it is not already there to run it directly from your
current working directory. The mpiexec command is typically used to directly
start multiple processes in parallel, where x is the number of processes running in
parallel.
To see how the library works, let us start with the simplest program you can run with
mpiexec :
```
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
print("The process %d is started" %rank)
```

To execute the code, we will have to use the mpiexec command. If you want to
start 2 processes in parallel, use this:
```
$ mpiexec -n 2 python mpi01.py
```

We will get the output of the two processes that looks like:
```
The process 0 is started
The process 1 is started
```

If, on the other hand, we want to start 6 in parallel, it will be sufficient to modify
the value of the parameter n passed on the command line, as demonstrated here:
```
$ mpiexec -n 6 python mpi01a.py
```

This will generate the following:
```
The process 2 is started
The process 5 is started
The process 1 is started
The process 4 is started
The process 3 is started
The process 0 is started
```

As we can see from the outputs, the rank order of the processes is not ordered but is
a random result that varies from execution to execution. While analyzing the code, the
comm parameter expresses the communicator, and defines the group of processes that
can communicate through the message passing mechanism :
```
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
```

Here, the rank is the identification number of the process within a group of communicating processes. That is, all the processes launched by the mpiexec command become
part of this communication group, and each of them is identified by a rank .

Parallelism of the Processes

As we have seen for the multiprocessing module, the processes allow the execution of the
code in parallel. We can perform the same tests with the mpi4py library. This time,
we will perform benchmarking by measuring the execution times. For this purpose, we
launch a program:

```
import time
```

Efficiency of Parallelism Based on the
Number of processors/cores

As for the efficiency of parallelism based on the number of processors or cores, different
time measurements can be made by varying the number of parallel processes. We will
use the following code:
```
import time
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
print("The process %d is started" %rank)
n = 0
for i in range(100000000):
n += i
print("The process %d is ended" %rank)
```

We will execute the code with mpiexec by varying the number of processors.

Main Applications of mpi4py

The mpi4py library is based on the message passing according to MPI standards.
Its applications in the world of parallel programming can be divided into three different
groups:

• Point-to-Point Communication
• Collective Communication
• Topologies

In the second half of the chapter, we will look at these applications through a series of
examples.

## 252 MAIN APPLICATIONS OF MPI4PY


<a id='p253'></a>
<!-- Página 253 -->

Point-to-Point Communication
Implementation

Point-to-point operations consist of an exchange of messages between two processes. In a
perfect world, each sending operation should be perfectly synchronized with the respective
receiving operation. Obviously, this is not the case, and the MPI implementation must be
able to preserve the data sent even when the sending process and the receiving process are
not synchronized. Typically, a buffer is used, which is transparent to the developer and
entirely managed by the mpi4py library.
The mpi4py module enables point-to-point communication through two functions:

• comm.send(data, receiver_process)
• comm.recv(sender_process)

The send() function sends data to the receiving process through its rank in the
communication group. The recv() function receives data from the sending process,
which is also identified by its communication group rank number as demonstrated here:
```
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
print("Process %s started" %rank)
if rank==0:
msg = "This is the message"
receiver = 1
comm.send(msg, dest=receiver)
print("Process 0 sent a message to %d" %receiver + ": %s" %msg)
elif rank==1:
source = 0
msg = comm.recv(source=source)
print("Process 1 received a message from %d" %source + ": %s" %msg)
```

You will run the preceding code in parallel by running the following shell command:
```
$ mpiexec -n 9 python programma01.py

253
```

Collective Communication Using
Data Broadcast

During parallel programming, we might find ourselves in a situation where it is necessary
to share the value of a certain variable at runtime among several processes or to distribute
different operations on variables, to which each process provides a partial solution. To
solve this kind of situation, tree communication groups are used (for example, process 0
sends data to processes 1 and 2 , which in turn will send it to processes 3,4,5,6…and so
on ).
```
A method of communication that involves all the processes that belong to a communi-
```

cator is called collective communication . Consequently, collective communication is
based on more than two processes. In this case, we can call it broadcast , where a single
process sends the same data to the processes (see Figure 3.4 ).
```
Figure 3.4: Broadcasting
This will read the data defined in process 0 defined as root and then it will distribute
```

it among all processes, including the root process itself:
```
from mpi4py import MPI
from mpi4py import MPI
import random
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
if rank == 0:
data = random.randint(1, 10)
else:
data=None
data = comm.bcast(data, root=0)
if rank == 1:
print("The square of %d is %d" %(data, data*data))
elif rank == 2:
print("Half of %d is %d" %(data, data/2))
elif rank == 3:
print("Double of %d is %d" %(data, data*2))
This code will generate the following result:
```

Collective Communication Using
Data Scattering

The scattering functionality is very similar to that of broadcast, but is slightly different.
While comm.bcast() sends the same type of data to all listening processes,
comm.scatter() sends portions of data in an array to different processes (see Figure
3.5 ).
```
Figure 3.5: Scattering
```

The comm.scatter() function takes the elements of the array and distributes
them among the processes based on their rank; so, the first element will be sent to process
0 , the second element to process 1 , and so on:
```
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
if rank == 0:
array = ['AAA','BBB','CCC','DDD']
else:
array = None
data = comm.scatter(array,root=0)
print("Process %d is working on %s element" %(rank,data))
```

This code will generate the following result:
```
$mpiexec -n 4 python mpi05a.py
Process 0 is working on AAA element
Process 1 is working on BBB element
Process 2 is working on CCC element
Process 3 is working on DDD element
```

Collective Communication Using
Data Gathering

The gathering function performs the inverse operation of scattering. In this case, all the
processes involved in the calculation send their portions of data to a receiving root process
that collects them at once (see Figure 3.6 ).
```
Figure 3.6: Gathering
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
if rank == 0:
data = 'AAA'
elif rank == 1:
data = 'BBB'
elif rank == 2:
data = 'CCC'
elif rank == 3:
data = 'DDD'
array = comm.gather(data, root=0)
if rank == 0:
print("The new array is %s " %array)
This code will generate the following result:
$mpiexec -n 4 python mpi06a.py
The new array is ['AAA', 'BBB', 'CCC', 'DDD']
This method of passing messages can be useful for parallel computing. Many algo-
```

rithms rely on calculations that can be broken down into smaller identical chunks . By
assigning each of them to a parallel process, you can effectively reduce execution times.
At the end of the calculation, many partial results will be obtained which will all be added
together to give a final result.
```
Let us take a simple example to see how this concept fits well with collective communi-
```

cation with gathering:
```
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
```

Reduction Operation

The reduction operation performed by comm.reduce() takes an array of input elements from each process and returns an array of output elements to the root process. The
output items contain the reduced result:
```
from mpi4py import MPI
import numpy as np
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
if rank == 0:
output = np.array([0,0,0,0])
elif rank == 1:
output = np.array([1,1,1,1])
elif rank == 2:
output = np.array([2,2,2,2])
elif rank == 3:
output = np.array([3,3,3,3])
print("Process %d. Sending %s" %(rank, output))
input = comm.reduce(output, root=0, op=MPI.SUM)
if rank == 0:
print("The result of the parallel computation is %s" %input)
```

This code will generate the following result:
```
$mpiexec -n 4 python mpi08a.py
Process 3. Sending [3 3 3 3]
Process 2. Sending [2 2 2 2]
Process 1. Sending [1 1 1 1]
Process 0. Sending [0 0 0 0]
The result of the parallel computation is [6 6 6 6]
```

Optimization of Communications
through Topologies

An interesting feature provided by MPI is the possibility to intervene in virtual topologies.
All communication between processes occurs through communication groups. So far,
by using MPI_COMM_WORLD , all processes are assigned to a group and each of them is
assigned a rank number starting from 0 up to n-1 , where n is the number of processes
launched in parallel execution.
```
The mpi4py library allows us to define a virtual topology for this communicator,
```

or the way in which ranks assigned can be redefined. By defining a virtual topology, each
node (process) will only be able to communicate with neighboring nodes in the virtual topology. In this way, we can improve the performance given the reduction in execution times.
In fact, in complex cases, as the ranks are randomly assigned to the various processes, the
messages could pass through many of them before reaching the correct destination, that is
the process for which this message was intended.
```
MPI provides two ways of building a topology:

```

• Cartesian
• Adjacency matrix

```
The first creates a Cartesian topology, while the second requires an adjacency matrix
```

of the graph we want to create.
```
In this example, we will use only the Cartesian topologies, through which it is possible
```

to build many topologies that are widely used as rings and toroids :
```
from mpi4py import MPI
comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
rank = comm.rank
comm_3D = comm.Create_cart(dims = [3,3,3], periods=[False,False,False],
```

reorder=False)
```
xyz = comm_3D.Get_coords(rank)
print ("In this 3D topology, process %s has coordinates %s " %(rank,xyz))

```

This code will generate the following result:
```
$mpiexec -n 27 python mpi09.py

273
```

As one of the processes is given, it is possible to know which processes are adjacent to it
via the following function:
```
shift(direction,displacement)
```

This function returns two integers, which correspond to the ranks of two adjacent processes on one of the Cartesian axes. The direction argument indicates in which direction
we want to know the neighbors, corresponding to the Cartesian axes. The direction range
is [0, n-1], where n is the size of the Cartesian mesh. So, in our case 0 will be Z ,
1 will be X , and 2 will be Y (based on the previous figure). The other argument
indicates when we need to move.
```
displacement (> 0: upwards shift, < 0: downwards shift) (integer)
```

Comparison of Threading and
Multiprocessing in Python:
Advantages and Disadvantages

By now, you should have gained a good understanding of threading and multiprocessing
techniques. Choosing which one to apply is fundamental in Python in order to develop
efficient applications and make the most of system resources, especially in multi-core environments. It is therefore important to analyze the differences between the two different
approaches, while highlighting the most suitable use cases and the practical implications for
optimizing performance. Before going into the heart of the matte, let us get an overview
of the fundamental characteristics that distinguish the two different approaches:

• Threading : Threading creates threads, which refer to the execution units that op-
```
erate within the same process. Threads share the same memory space and can
communicate with each other easily as they are part of the same process. However,
in Python, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) limits the concurrent execution of threads
in CPU-bound applications (that require a lot of processing power), causing a serialized
execution. Despite this limitation, threading is beneficial for I/O-bound applications
that frequently interact with external resources such as files, databases, or networks.
```

• Multiprocessing: Unlike threading, multiprocessing creates separate processes,
```
each with its own memory space and an independent instance of the Python interpreter. This approach bypasses the GIL, while allowing CPU-bound operations to be
executed in parallel on multiple cores. However, since they are separate processes,
data is not directly shared between processes. This levels an additional cost on the
communication between processes.

```

It is evident that the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is intrinsic to the structure of
Python, while playing a key role. This synchronization mechanism limits the execution of
concurrent threads to a single thread at a time, even on multi-core processors. This means
that while one thread executes Python code, the other threads must wait for the GIL to be
released, even if CPU resources are available. This limits the effectiveness of threading
in CPU-bound Python applications. However, the GIL does not have a significant impact
on I/O-bound applications, since during input/output operations, the GIL is released, while

```
277
```


<a id='p278'></a>
<!-- Página 278 -->

278 COMPARISON OF THREADING AND MULTIPROCESSING IN PYTHON: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTA

allowing other threads to advance. Therefore, the choice of threading or multiprocessing
often depends on the nature of the application:

• I/O-Bound Applications : For example, web servers or web scrapers benefit from
```
threading, since many I/O operations can be handled simultaneously.
```

• CPU-Bound Applications : Data-intensive applications such as scientific calculations
```
or image transformations require multiprocessing to take advantage of parallelism
across multiple cores.

```

Advantages of Threading

• Memory Sharing : Since threads share the same memory space, they can directly
```
access the same variables and data. This makes it easy for them to communicate with
each other without having to implement complex communication mechanisms.
```

• Lightweight: Creating threads is less expensive in terms of system resources than
```
creating processes, so that it can be a more efficient option when working on I/O-bound
tasks.
```

• Suitable for I/O-Bound Tasks: Threading is particularly advantageous for tasks such
```
as network operations or disk reads/writes, where the CPU is often waiting (blocked)
for input/output.

```

Disadvantages of Threading

• Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) : In Python, the GIL prevents threads from executing
```
code on multiple CPU cores at the same time. As a result, threading cannot take
advantage of the CPU’s parallelism.
```

• Data safety : Since threads share the same memory, there is a risk of race conditions
```
and other synchronization problems, which make it more difficult to manage concurrency.

```

Advantages of Multiprocessing

• Full CPU Usage : Multiprocessing allows you to bypass the GIL as each process has
```
its own Python interpreter, which allows you to use the various CPU cores.
```

• Process Isolation: Since each process has its own memory space, data is isolated
```
and there is no risk of direct interference between processes. This simplifies the
management of concurrency.

```

Disadvantages of Multiprocessing

• Higher Resource Consumption: Creating processes is more expensive than creating
```
threads, since each process has its own memory and context. This can result in a
higher consumption of RAM and system resources.
```


<a id='p279'></a>
<!-- Página 279 -->

```
279

```

• More Complex Communication: Communication between processes requires inter-
```
process (IPC) mechanisms such as pipes or queues, which can be complex and add
latency.
```

• Not Suitable for I/O-Bound Tasks: When compared to threads, multiprocessing is
```
less efficient for I/O operations as processes commonly occupy resources while waiting
for their completion.

```

Now we will show two examples of Python code where we will compare threading and
multiprocessing modules on two different types of tasks:

• I/O bound, where threading is more efficient
• CPU bound, where multiprocessing is more advantageous

```
In the first example, we simulate an I/O-bound task using time.sleep to mimic a
```

network or disk read/write operation. Here, the CPU does not play a fundamental role.
```
We will define two different functions for this purpose. In the threading_example()
```

function, we create 5 threads that execute io_bound_task where each thread waits
for 1 second for the I/O task to be executed. In the multiprocessing_example()
function, we will create 5 separate processes to execute the same operation. Since the task
is I/O bound and does not require much CPU, threading should be faster and lighter than
multiprocessing, since the threads can perform the wait without interference from the GIL.
```
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time
def io_bound_task():
print(f"{threading.current_thread().name} is working…")
time.sleep(i)
print(f"{threading.current_thread().name} ended its work.")
# Threading
def threading_example():
start_time = time.time()
threads = []
for _ in range(5):
thread = threading.Thread(target=io_bound_task)
threads.append(thread)
thread.start()
for thread in threads:
thread.join()
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Time with threading: {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")
# Multiprocessing
def multiprocessing_example():
start_time = time.time()
```


<a id='p280'></a>
<!-- Página 280 -->

280 COMPARISON OF THREADING AND MULTIPROCESSING IN PYTHON: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTA

```
processes = []
for _ in range(5):
process = multiprocessing.Process(target=io_bound_task)
processes.append(process)
process.start()
for process in processes:
process.join()
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Time with multiprocessing: {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")

if __name__ == '__main__':
print("Execution of I/O-bound task:")
print("Using threading…")
threading_example()
print("Using multiprocessing…")
multiprocessing_example()
```

```
In the second example, we will define a CPU-bound task this time, where each worker has
```

to compute prime numbers in a specific range. Here, multiprocessing will be more advantageous as it bypasses the GIL by exploiting the multiple cores available in the CPU in a parallel manner. Again, we will use two different functions to differentiate between the two different approaches. In the threading_example_cpu() function, we create 4 threads
to compute prime numbers up to 10000, while in the multiprocessing_example_cpu()
function, we create 4 separate processes to perform the same operation. In this case,
multiprocessing should be faster since each process can execute the code on one CPU core
without interference from the GIL, which makes the processing of a CPU-bound task like a
mathematical calculation more efficient.
```
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time
def cpu_bound_task(n):
count = 0
for i in range(2, n):
for j in range(2, i):
if 1 % j == 0:
break
else:
count += 1
print(f"Prime numbers found: {count}")
# Threading
def threading_example_cpu():
start_time = time.time()
threads = []
for _ in range(4):
thread = threading.Thread(target=cpu_bound_task, args=(10000,))
threads.append(thread)
thread.start()
for thread in threads:
thread.join()
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Time with threading: {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")
# Multiprocessing
def multiprocessing_example_cpu:
start_time = time.time()
processes = []
for _ in range(4):
process = multiprocessing.Process(target=cpu_bound_task, args=(10000,))

processes.append(process)
```

Improving Performance with
Advanced Multiprocessing

Returning to the multiprocessing technique, we will now expand the general framework
by adding more advanced concepts such as CPU affinity. When implementing highperformance CPU-bound applications, simple parallelization via multiprocessing may not
be enough to optimize the use of system resources. In these situations, advanced techniques such as configuring CPU affinity allow you to further improve performance by distributing the workload more efficiently.
```
To fully understand the importance of CPU affinity, it is useful to consider how processes
```

are normally managed by the operating system (OS). The operating system assigns available
processes to CPUs based on the availability of cores by default to redistribute the load as
needed. While this approach is effective, in CPU-bound intensive applications where
processes perform complex calculations, moving a process from one CPU to another can
incur overhead due to the need to reload the CPU caches. Setting CPU affinity for each
process can reduce this overhead, and improve execution speed and efficiency.
```
CPU affinity is a configuration that assigns one or more specific CPU cores to a given
```

process. When a process is limited to certain cores, it reduces the risk of migration to other
CPUs, thus minimizing context and cache management costs. This advanced technique
offers several advantages in computationally intensive applications such as:

• Minimization of Context Costs: By keeping a process on the same core, the cost of con-
```
text switching between different CPUs is avoided, which improves cache coherence.
```

• Reduction of Latency Times: Computationally intensive processes benefit from re-
```
duced execution times, since they avoid interruptions caused by dynamic CPU reassignment.
```

• Optimization of Multi-Core Resource Use: Explicitly assigning cores to different pro-
```
cesses can help balance the load between CPU cores, thereby improving the overall
efficiency of the system.

In Python, configuring CPU affinity is not natively supported by the multiprocessing li-
```

brary, but can be handled via modules such as os for Unix-based systems or third-party
libraries on Windows. The following is an example of CPU affinity configuration on a
Linux system.

```

```


which cores can run a process.

```
Let us write an example for CPU affinity configuration. In this code, each process
```

is created and executed separately using multiprocessing.Process . The
os.sched_setaffinity function assigns each process to a specific CPU core, while alternating between available cores to distribute the load.
```
import os
import multiprocessing
import time
def cpu_bound_task(task_id):
"""Simulation of an intensive operation that requires a lot of CPU resources.""

print(f"Process {task_id} assigned to CPU {os.sched_getaffinity(0)}")

# CPU-bound Task (e.g.,calculating a sum for large numbers)
result = sum(i * i for i in range(10**6))
print(f"Process {task_id} finished, result: {result}")
if __name__ == '__main__':
processes = []
# Configure processes with different CPU affinity
for i in range(4):
process = multiprocessing.Process(target=cpu_bound_task, args=(i,))
process.start()
# Assign each process to a specific CPU
cpu_core = i % os.cpu_count()
os.sched_setaffinity(process.pid, {cpu_core}) # Assign the process
```

to a specific CPU
```
processes.append(process)
for process in processes:
process.join()
print("All processes are completed.")
```

Implementing Job Scheduling with
Multiprocessing

Another advanced method to improve the efficiency of parallel execution is job scheduling. In contexts like those discussed in this book, where tasks are numerous and require
an optimized use of available resources, it is essential to coordinate the execution of tasks
efficiently.
Job scheduling consists of planning and distributing the execution of tasks so that system
resources are used at their best, maintaining optimal execution times and balancing the load
among the available cores. Python offers several scheduling features through multiprocessing such as Pool for process management, asynchronous functions ( apply_async
, map_async ) and queue mechanisms. In Python, job scheduling through multiprocessing can be divided into some key operations:
```
Creating and Managing Processes: Through multiprocessing.Process , it is
```

possible to start single independent processes, but in environments with many tasks, a pool
of processes is more efficient.
Dynamic Scheduling: Asynchronous functions like apply_async allow you to
schedule tasks and distribute them dynamically to available processes.
```
Queue and Load Balancing: Queues and data structures like Queue allow you to manage
```

a large number of tasks, while distributing them gradually and in a balanced way.
```
Let us start with a basic approach to see how Pool facilitates job scheduling. In the
```

previous sections, we have already introduced multiprocessing.Pool in an introductory context on its use. Now let us see how to use it in a more advanced context. This
module provides an interface to create and manage a pool of processes, which will allow you
to automatically distribute tasks to available processes. Using this, you can easily scale an
application on multi-core systems without having to manually manage each process. In
particular, we will use it through asynchronous functions like Pool.apply_async to
distribute tasks asynchronously. Let us see an example where we will use this method to
schedule tasks that will be executed as soon as a process in the pool becomes available:
```
import multiprocessing
import time
def process_task(task_id):
"""Simulation of a task that takes time to complete."""
```

```
In addition to Pool.apply_async() , the module provides additional job schedul-
```

ing tools . Pool.map and Pool.map_async are particularly useful methods for managing a series of homogeneous tasks, such as repetitive operations on a dataset.
map executes tasks in parallel and waits for all processes to complete, while map_asyn
c allows you to schedule tasks asynchronously. Let us develop some sample code
where map executes tasks simultaneously and waits for all of them to complete before
continuing, while blocking the program execution. map_async starts tasks, and allows the program to continue execution until the results are requested with .get()
.
```
import multiprocessing
import time
def square(number):
"""Simulates a long calculation operation to square a number."""
time.sleep(1)
return number * number
if __name__ == "__main__":
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
# Synchronous execution with map (all tasks run in parallel and awaited)

with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
results_sync = pool.map(square, numbers)
print("Synchronous results:", results_sync)
# Asynchronous execution with map_async
with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
result_async = pool.map_async(square, numbers)
# .get() blocks until all asynchronous tasks are completed
results_async = result_async.get()
print("Asynchronous results:", results_async)
```

Introduction

Previously, we have looked at concurrent programming based on threads and the threading
module in particular. The limitations imposed by the GIL pose major problems which will
have to be resolved if we want to work with threads in Python. This feature of Python,
therefore, imposes thread concurrency, which is an inevitable limitation compared to parallel programming. Thus, in Python, a concurrent programming approach becomes indispensable for managing tasks involving I/O communications where unpredictable waiting
times have to be managed in conjunction with other tasks. In this chapter, we return to
this type of programming through alternative approaches like the asynchronous model
and the AsyncIO library .
