Meteorology

Meteorology is based on extraordinarily complex mathematical models that take into
account numerous climatic and environmental factors. These changes are observed over
time to make forecasts on the weather as correctly as possible.
```
It is therefore clear that in this domain, it is necessary to use extraordinarily powerful
```

computers based on parallel computing and employ Numeric Weather Prediction (

## NWP ).

```
NWP is a weather forecasting method based on a series of dynamic equations describ-
```

ing the flow of fluids. This system is very mathematically complex and it is tedious devise
solutions on the basis of mere equations. In order to be submitted to computers, these
equations must first be converted into numerical methods through a series of processes.
Parameterizations are made and initial and boundary conditions are imposed. Unfortunately, these steps introduce approximations, along with omissions, parameter estimates,
and other factors that simplify the calculation, but also introduce numerous inaccuracies at
the same time.
```
The purpose of NWP is to simulate the atmosphere of a geographical area in its temporal
```

evolution to predict climatic trends. The volume occupied by the atmosphere covering
the geographical area is divided into a grid of three-dimensional points that define its
resolution. Advances in parallel computational processing increase the resolution of the
model and the computation speed, which generates results. The higher the resolution
of the model, the more accurate predictions will be. However, manipulating models of
this level is highly challenging. Despite the increase in resolution and simulation speed,
current algorithms can reach their limits due to the communication requirements of the
algorithms used to solve the equations that predict how the weather evolves over time.
```
At present, these algorithms combine computational parallelism with geographic paral-
```

lelism. The geographical area under analysis is divided into overlapping parts and each
part is assigned to a different processor. During the forecast calculation, each processor will have to exchange data that concerns the overlapping area with other processors
involved in the calculation to account for the climatic effects on neighboring areas.
```
The increase in resolution and speed has led to the analysis of ever smaller geographical
```

areas. However, expanding the area of overlap between various processors also increases
the exchange of information and reduces the model’s performance.
```
Another critical point of the NWP model is the parameterized part. There are many
```

physical processes in meteorology that cannot be predicted directly (see Figure 7.1 ).


of reflected waves of various shapes and intensities is obtained to be detected, recorded in
the form of data, and then used to extrapolate a model that can reconstruct the underlying
layers of the soil.

Astrophysics

Another branch of science that uses parallel programming to make simulations is astrophysics.
```
The behavior and evolution of a star is in the concern of astrophysics and is based on
```

simulations that use complex physical laws which consider hydrodynamics and magneto
hydrodynamics . The reference system has spherical geometry and the model uses spectral codes to subdivide physical quantities on the basis of spherical harmonics in orthogonal
directions and Chebyshev polynomials along the radial direction. It is clear that these calculations are complex and can be processed only via high-performance computing systems
like massively parallel architectures (supercomputers).
```
The results obtained from this type of simulation have proved to be very accurate and
```

have allowed enormous progress in astrophysics .


proach are called star-in-a-box . These simulations are based on a different model,
which is in turn based on Cartesian geometry. Here, a star is enclosed inside a cubic box
(see Figure 7.5 ). One can obtain accurate results via the scientific libraries provided
by Python such as SciPy , NumPy , and Matplotlib . Historically, libraries like
PyPar were used to facilitate parallel implementations in Python, but since PyPar is no
longer maintained, the modern standard for distributed-memory parallelism in Python is
mpi4py , which provides full bindings to the MPI (Message Passing Interface) standard.
```

```

considered impossible to counter. The explosion of a supernova , the movement
of galaxies with their probable collision and merger, and the behavior of a black hole are
complex problems and need models with enormous computing power to create simulations
based on them.

matter that orbits and then collapses into black holes lines up with the latter. This demonstration was only possible with the permission to simulate a powerful supercomputer. It
is therefore clear that with the growth of computing power, many other problems that have

Resource exploration is a method of collecting and managing information about energy
resources such as oil , natural gas , and so on. Computers help discover and manage
such resources. Oil and gas companies are exploring every possible method to increase
the probability of finding hydrocarbons under the ground.

supercomputers typically rely on combinations of AMD EPYC CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, or similar
high-performance components.

```
This particular technique boosts the performance and calculation speed of such a pro-
```

cessor. Bubba belongs to the geo-processing company DownUnder GeoSolutions and is
used to perform these calculations. From this, we can understand how every research
sector interested in the business is very sensitive to the importance of simulations and the
parallel computing on the basis of which they are processed.

Engineering

Finite Element Analysis ( FEA ) is the simulation of any given physical phenomenon
using a numerical technique called the Finite Element Method ( FEM ).
```
Engineers use FEA simulations to reproduce the behavior of virtual prototypes under
```

various conditions without physically building them. From the data collected from these
simulations, it is possible to optimize the choice of components , their material , and
shape , without having to physically create and test them each time and wasting resources.
To do this, however, it is necessary to use mathematical models that simulate reality as
closely as possible. The models should also be able to quantify the effects of physical and
structural phenomena like heat transfer , wave propagation , resistance to pressure
, and so on. Most of these models are described by Partial Differential Equations (
PDEs ).
```
The Finite Element Analysis method is the technique that has been successful at man-
```

aging calculations and has provided excellent results. Therefore, it is clear that to carry
out an increasingly accurate and efficient FEA, high-performance computers that use parallel computing are required. In an FEA, an extremely large number of partial differential
equations are solved concurrently and then processed in parallel.
```
To perform simulations, a mesh consisting of millions of small elements that form the
```

shape of the structure needs to be created.
```
Calculations are then made on each individual element. After combining the individual
```

results, you get the final one that describes the whole structure. This means that an
approximation of the interpolation is introduced in the space between the values obtained
```
from the points (nodes) that describe the elements.
In other words, you know the value of some points, but not all. Interpolation can
```

be improved by using increasingly complex systems, or by increasing the number of finite
elements in the analysis. This is done at the expense of computing power, with a request
for more complex calculations and memory. It is therefore clear that to improve the
performance and accuracy of these simulations, it is necessary to enhance the calculation
tool on which it is performed.
```
The advances obtained in parallel computing are in fact leading to improvements in FEA,
```

as well as the results obtained from simulations.
```
As far as FEM methods in Python are concerned, we have many projects and libraries
```

available, which are:
```
Figure 7.9: SfePy Official Website with Some Examples
```

Medicine and Drug Discovery

Parallel computing is also used in medicine, especially in image processing . Diagnostic
devices that scan the human body and brain use advanced technologies to produce images.
One of the most widely used techniques in this field is Magnetic Resonance Imaging
( MRI ) reconstruction, which is used to reconstruct magnetic resonance images and for
tasks such as brain fiber tracking. Similarly, Computed Tomography (CT) uses parallel
reconstruction algorithms for X-ray images.
```
Python, as a scientific programming language, offers several widely used tools for this
```

area. Libraries such as nilabel (for reading and writing medical image formats),
DiPy (for diffusion imaging and tractography), and SigPy (for advanced reconstruction
algorithms) provide a rich ecosystem for MRI research and analysis.
```
In particular, SigPy fully exploits the potential of parallel computing on both CPUs
```

and GPUs. It offers a comprehensive set of tools for signal processing tasks and includes
a dedicated module for MRI applications, sigpy.mri , which is specifically designed
for magnetic resonance image reconstruction.
```
To install the latter you can use the Anaconda platform and the following code:
conda install -c frankong sigpy
# (optional for plot support) conda install matplotlib
# (optional for CUDA support) conda install cupy
# (optional for MPI support) conda install mpi4py
However, parallel signal processing techniques are also being adopted in other diagnos-
```

tic sectors. Patients with neuromuscular or cardiorespiratory disease need constant
monitoring. This constant monitoring produces a large amount of data in the form of signals which contain useful information of different types and have to be processed as soon
as possible. So, we must use signal processing algorithms adapted for this type of application. A peculiar feature is that the data needs to be processed in real-time, which means
that the window of time provided is rather brief. The data produced by monitoring
consist of bio signals of different types (generally electrocardiogram , respiration ,
electroencephalogram , and electromyogram ), that are acquired simultaneously. Their
processing to extract useful information is not trivial and requires considerable time. It is
clear that the classical approach generates delays and inefficiencies which could be critical,
given that we are talking about human health.
```
Therefore the transition to parallel processing is an indispensable step to make these
```

current monitoring systems more efficient and capable of giving answers in real-time

```
575
```

<!-- Página 576 -->

576 MEDICINE AND DRUG DISCOVERY

for prompt intervention. Detecting sudden changes in the patient’s vital signs must be
accurate and fast enough to prevent serious complications.
```
In Python, one of the earlier libraries designed for biosignal processing was BioSPPy,
```

a toolbox that provided various signal processing and pattern recognition methods for analyzing common biosignals such as PPG, ECG, EDA, EEG, EMG, and respiration. However,
BioSPPy is no longer actively maintained. A more modern and actively developed alternative is NeuroKit2, which offers a wide range of tools for biosignal processing and analysis.
NeuroKit2 can be easily installed from PyPI using the pip command:
```
pip install neurokit2
Even the research sector makes intensive use of complex algorithms in their activity in
```

applications like drug discovery and genomics. It is clear that the conversion of these
algorithms from serial to parallel and the use of calculation systems (supercomputers) is
undergoing a phase of development.

Drug Discovery

Drug discovery is one of the most expensive, time-demanding, and challenging tasks
pharmaceutical companies face. Identification and optimization of molecules or peptides
are done on huge scales of available compounds. The molecules must meet particular
requirements such as having high binding affinity and specificity with an associated target,
which is generally an enzyme ( molecular docking technique ). The latter is linked to a
disease and its activation-deactivation gives the molecule its efficacy as a drug. However,
the molecule must also have favorable pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic
properties, otherwise, it can be unassimilated or metabolized too quickly and not reach
the target enzyme. The simulation of such an analysis requires a copious amount of
computational resources and time that the introduction of parallel computing becomes very
necessary.
```
Therefore, the pharmaceutical industry is giving a strong impetus to the development
```

and innovation of the current analysis techniques and the calculators on which they are
processed.
```
Drug discovery is a huge market and requires huge economic efforts. Despite this, it
```

has been calculated that only one compound out of 10,000 proposed by Research and
Development will prove to be a successful drug. So, it is clear that speeding up and
lightening the simulation and analysis phases of a potential drug will reduce expenses.
```
Molecular docking consists of sampling the possible spatial configurations that the
```

molecule can assume and calculating the scoring functions for each of these configurations
when it is binding to the enzyme.
```
This activity is computationally very expensive, but it can be easily parallelized. Also,
```

many algorithms used in the evaluation of a drug can be parallelized, thus increasing the
performance of the whole process.
```
When these techniques are applied to supercomputers, there is an increase in the calcu-
```

lation speed and therefore the time needed for the extraction of potential drugs reduces.
```
However, research also opens the landscape for many other innovations.
Figure 7.10: Acellera Web Page for Computable Drug Discovery
There are many software packages for Molecular Docking , including Autodock ,
```

which is made in C/C++ and has recently upgraded into a new version, called AutodockGPU . The new version greatly exploits the potential of graphics cards. In fact, it has

Genomics

As far as genomics is concerned, here too the massive use of supercomputers based on
parallel computing is necessary. The study of an organism’s genome requires manipulating
and processing very large amount of data and information, which is difficult to manage if
there are no algorithms that work in parallel.
```
Genomics is the most representative of bioinformatics disciplines as it compares struc-
```

tures such as DNA sequences , genes , and RNA between different organisms. However, the data runs in enormous dimensions (Terabytes) so much so that it can be defined
as Biological Big Data . Without parallel computing, a single experiment could stretch
over several weeks, if not months. It is therefore essential that parallelization and HPC
techniques are applied in order to reduce these processing times and make it possible to
manage, process and analyze this type of data.
```
However, the integration of algorithms used in bioinformatics with parallel computing
```

is not a simple matter and is still being studied. There are two main approaches to address
this challenge. Historically, software such as FASTA , BLAST , HMMER , ClustalW
, and RaxML have been redesigned to leverage parallel computing, for example with MPI
(see Figure 7.11 ). In modern genomics pipelines, however, the standard tools include
Bowtie2, BWA, STAR, GATK, and minimap2 , which are designed to efficiently handle the
massive scale of next-generation sequencing data.
```
An alternative is to use distributed systems, or clouds, in which pipelines are developed
```

for bioinformatics calculations and can be represented as workflows.
```
Figure 7.11: BLAST Official Page
There are workflow systems such as Tavaxy , Pegasus , Swift/T , and SciCumulus
```

that can manage bioinformatics processing in distributed infrastructures.
```
As for Python, there is the pyrpipe library, which is designed to process RNA-
```

Seq data by developing computational pipelines entirely in Python. This library can be
used both on local computers and in HPC environments and can be easily integrated into
workflow management systems such as Snakemake and Nextflow .
```
This library can be easily installed on the Anaconda platform:
conda install -c bioconda pyrpipe
Along with pyrpipe , the Anaconda distribution includes a huge amount of
```

bioinformatics-specific libraries, all gathered in a dedicated repository called bioconda (
https://anaconda.org/bioconda/repo ).
```
Furthermore, always on Anaconda , there is another library called BioPython which
```

Entertainment – Games and Movies

After so many applications in various scientific and industrial sectors, it will be surprising

strongly pushed for the development of particular processors that enhance games and 3D
environments. Games are constantly evolving and have now reached enormous levels in
which the images flow smoothly, are rich in interactive features (often guided by AI), and
are a part of increasingly realistic scenarios. It is in fact here that we discover the potential
of the highly parallel structure of graphics cards.

Game Engines

At the heart of most games lies a complex structure called a game engine .
```
There are several game-engine models that are distributed in the market to make video
```

games. Among the most important are:

• The Unreal Engine
• Unity
• Godot

```
These powerful game engines are easy to use and have intelligent features that can be
```

used to create beautiful applications and ensure realistic gaming experiences (see Figure
7.12 ).
```
Figure 7.12: Unreal Engine Official Web Page
For developers, the provided user interfaces allow them to develop games in a simple
```

way, while leveraging the strengths of powerful technologies in both graphics (supported
by GPUs) and learning (AI). This yields the possibility of obtaining fluid movements of
subjects in three-dimensional settings. These game engines are constantly evolving and
incorporate within them all possible innovations in the field of parallel programming.
Often, these technologies are then reused in other areas, as seen previously.
```
The power of game engines is also based on 3D rendering . It allows players to have
```

realistic gaming experience and creates images starting from three-dimensional modeling.
```
The three-dimensional models of objects that make up the virtual environment created
```

by the game engine undergo a texturing phase. Two-dimensional images are applied to
cover the surface of these objects, while giving them a material appearance, with a calculated sheen based on the orientation of the lighting. Other effects such as shadows are
added and in the end; the 2D image is created, which as a photograph, converts virtual reality into a realistic image.
```
Using more powerful calculators generates better results and creates more realistic im-
```

ages. Furthermore, these images will have to be generated for each frame of the video
game, which, like the frames of a movie, will have to flow smoothly. Therefore, it is
easy to understand the demands this technology exerts on computing power. In addition
to this, there are the necessary calculations for the management of sound, AI, network, and
memory.
```
Parallel computing is a powerful tool for optimizing the underlying processes in a game
```

engine. The most powerful game engines currently use CPU cores and GPUs through

```
585
```

586 GAME ENGINES




```
Figure 78:


```

multithreading . In our book, we have seen that Python does not handle multithreading
on CPUs well, and in fact, these game engines are based on programming languages such as
C# and C++ that allow you to apply multithreading on CPUs.
```
Figure 7.13: Unity Official Web Page
In the Unity game engine (see Figure 7.13 ), multithreading is applied to execute
```

rendering processes in parallel across threads. Parallel execution of multiple threads
greatly reduces the execution time of processes within a frame. Therefore, more frames
can be generated per second and the games will be smoother . This is where GPUs come
into play, as their architecture is designed to resolve the calculation of pixel textures more
efficiently than a CPU would. Furthermore, the enormously parallel internal structure
allows this computation to be assigned to a large number of threads simultaneously, thereby
lightening the workload and reducing execution times.
```
Furthermore, the CPU is free to carry out further tasks in the meantime. Since CPUs
```

are powerful in mathematical calculations, they are used in parallel to perform calculations
that make the 3D environment even more realistic. The behavior of objects, the effects of
shocks, and the waves transmitted in the water, the responses to user interactions, and even
the intelligence of Non-Player Characters ( NPCs ) are processed by algorithms destined
for the CPU, whose cores allocate many threads for parallel computing.
As mentioned for Python, there are no full-fledged game engines comparable to Unreal
Engine or Unity. Instead, most options are available as libraries. PyGame remains

```
In addition to PyGame, there are other Python-native frameworks such as Pyglet ,
```

Designing a Parallel Game Engine

There is a wonderful article on the Intel website, which is titled Designing the Framework
of a Parallel Game Engine . You can access it via:
```
https://www.intel.com/content/dam/develop/external/us/en/documents/designing-a-parallel-
```

game-engine-593584.pdf
```
The article illustrates the steps involved in designing a possible game engine. It can be
```

a good stimulus to develop a new game engine in Python.
```
A good design for a game engine makes the most of all available processors. We have
```

seen that other game engines leverage multithreading on CPUs to achieve this purpose.
In Python, since we do not have this possibility, we can use multiprocessing . As far as
GPU is concerned, we have seen that Python is not affected by major limitations compared
to other programming languages.
```
A game engine works on a processing loop aimed at creating one frame after another.
```

Each frame is the result of a series of processes that include the movement of objects in
three-dimensional space and includes texturing , rendering , and user interactions
. It is clear that the generation of the frame leads to a serial execution of the game.
Serial execution refers to when the frames are generated in an ordered sequence consecutively. However, between the generation of one frame and another, the potential of
parallel computing can be leveraged to the maximum possible degree. Between the two
frames, threads and processes spawn and work in parallel to perform all necessary tasks,
thereby reducing processing time. Then the generation of the frame will occur when all
the threads or processes have finished executing to give a result. The exchange of information between them at this moment reduces the synchronization load significantly and
prompts the system to react more quickly from one frame to another.
```
The article shows two execution modes:

```

1. The Lock Step Mode shown in Figure 7.14 :
```
Figure 7.14: Lock Step Mode

```

2. The Free Step Mode , where not all the components must necessarily synchronize
```
at each frame step, but can extend over several cycles (see Figure 7.15 ).
Figure 7.15: Free Step Mode
```


stalling all these libraries, such as a series of specific virtual environments like the ones

library, clean and manipulate it according to your needs, and analyze it to extract useful

data in a few seconds or even less, depending on the computing power of your system.
But however powerful and efficient your system may be, sooner or later you will need to

Therefore, while trying to import such data, you would get an error message. Furthermore, with the increase in the size of DataFrames the rise in complex procedures for data
processing, execution times will lengthen considerably. This might be due to the underlying algorithms, but it also depends on computer resources which will gradually become
more scarce as incoming data increases in volume.
You must wonder how to proceed in this case as you arrive at a crisis point. The good
news is that the situation can be improved by measuring the scale of the problem. The
best solution, therefore, will include distributing data across distant systems and not stay
limited only to leveraging parallel computing. Among the systems that we have already
seen in the book, distributed systems can meet these needs in the best way. Systems
composed of multiple computing systems with their respective clusters work best for a data

Dask Library

Dask is a flexible library that allows you to extend many libraries such as Pandas ,
NumPy , Scikit-learn , and many others, on distributed systems for parallel computing
in Python. These libraries are the staple for anyone working with data analysis in Python.
Dask uses the same syntax , methods , and operating modes as these libraries.
In this way, users of these libraries will be able to use their codes by extending them with
Dask with minimal changes. Hence, scaling the code from a single-machine system to
distributed systems becomes more rapid with Dask.
```
Thus, Dask allows us to build distributed applications to scale up in just a few steps,
```

that is, it facilitates transition from a purely serial system to one with multiple processing
systems in parallel. This can also be referred to as scaling out , which means that
execution can be transferred to external distributed systems like the cloud.
```
Dask is conceptually split into two distinct parts:

```

• Dynamic Task Scheduling
• Big Data Collections

```
Dynamic task scheduling is used to optimize the calculations in a distributed system.
```

It converts the Python code containing functions, methods, and definitions of objects into
equivalent operations for parallel computing just like Pandas, but much more efficiently.
```
Big Data collections , on the other hand, are all series of objects containing data.
```

These are very similar to NumPy arrays and DataFrames, which are instead designed to
be distributed on clusters. These collections also preserve the interfaces of original data
structures, as well as the names of the methods used, the parameters passed, and the syntax
of the operations used on these objects.
```
In summary, Dask provides an extension to distributed systems with highly parallelized
```

DataFrames and arrays. It does so while maintaining the same syntax of the original
libraries to reuse the existing code and extend it to parallel computing in a simple and rapid
way. Furthermore, once the code is integrated with Dask, it can work on clusters with over
1,000 cores, as well as on a single processor system. In this case, Dask will optimize the
execution of the code as per the processing environment.
```
The operation of Dask can be summarized in Figure 8.3 as follows :
Figure 8.3: Operation Diagram of the Dask Library
Dask provides three different components:

611
```


<a id='p612'></a>
<!-- Página 612 -->

612




```
Figure 85:


```

• Big Data Collections : At a high level , this data structure is very similar to the
```
corresponding objects present in other libraries, such as the DataFrame in Pandas.
At a low level , they are designed to manage parallel computing in distributed systems.
```

• Task Graphs : They are generated by Dask from Big Data collections, as well as from
```
the operations to be performed on them. They divide these operations into smaller
parts called tasks, which will then be distributed to the various processors of the
system called the workers, who will have the task to run in parallel.
```

• Dynamic Task Scheduler : This component distributes tasks to available workers.

<!-- Página 613 -->

One of the peculiar characteristics of Dask is to extend data structures like the DataFrame
of the pandas library and enable NumPy arrays to work efficiently in distributed
systems. Dask offers a set of deployable objects called Collections, which include:

• Dask Array
• Dask DataFrame

```
Dask DataFrame is represented by many small DataFrame pandas that live in a
```

cluster . When you interact with Dask DataFrame, the functions and methods you
call are converted into smaller functions that run in parallel on multiple smaller Pandas
DataFrames.
```
Dask Array is represented by smaller NumPy arrays that live in your cluster. When
```

you interact with the Dask Array, the functions and methods you call are converted into
smaller functions that run in parallel on smaller NumPy arrays.
```
Now, let us look at these concepts in more detail. We will create a new Python 3
```

Notebook on Jupyter and in the first cell, we will import the libraries and modules we will
need. This is shown through the following code:
```

import pandas as pd
import dask.dataframe as dd
import dask.array as da
We will execute the cell and then insert the code in the next one. First, let us see how
```

we can create a simple pandas DataFrame which will be compared to the Dask DataFrame.
This is indicated as:
```
df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(60).reshape(10,6))
df
Running the cell will generate the result shown in Figure 8.9 (the values change because
```

they are random):


columns and ten records . This is an example, but in reality, DataFrames are generally
valued using a CSV file containing the data to be imported. There are many data sources
on the web that provide CSV files full of precious data to be imported and analyzed.

Methods on Collections

Now that we know how to define the most common collections like DataFrame and Array,
```
let us see how to apply methods to them. The nomenclature and syntax of the methods
```

should be the same (or almost) as the corresponding methods of the original libraries.
```
For example, if we want to calculate the average of the first column of the pandas DataFrame,
```

we would write:
```
df[1].mean()
As a result, the average will be:
0.42944239885994107
Therefore, as far as the Dask DataFrame is concerned, things should not change much
```

and should look like:
```
m = ddf[1].mean()
In this case, the function is assigned to a variable. As we have seen, the same rule
```

also applies to the methods in DataFrame. The methods are not executed until the
compute() function is called on the invoked method. To execute the method, we
have to write:
```
m.compute()
The same result was obtained with the pandas DataFrame, which was:
0.42944239885994107
If you want to calculate the average of the values contained within the array, just write:
mm = np.mean(darr)
This calculation will be performed only when the compute() method is invoked
```

through:
```
mm.compute()
This will give the following result:
4.52
Now, let us analyze the reason for this strange behavior of Dask and what actually takes
```

place behind it.




```
625
```

Computing and Task Graphs

As seen before, the difference between the Dask library and traditional libraries like Pandas
and NumPy is their behavior. Dask is a lazy library and we have seen that Dask enhances
a data structure later and not while defining the concerned collection. It builds a data
structure while defining it, which will be populated later. The same goes for the invocation
of methods, which is never followed by the calculation but remains pending through its
assignment to a variable.
```
The population of a collection and the execution of a method occurs only when the
```

compute() method is invoked in the code on the relative object defined previously.
This operation is called computing and it occurs differently than in Pandas or NumPy.
As you must have noticed, the object is partitioned/divided into different parts while it is
being defined. Each portion will then be assigned a task which in turn will be assigned
to a different worker. The calculations within a collection will then be valued and executed in parallel. For instance, the different portions of a DataFrame will be populated
and processed in parallel , which reduces the overall processing time. With small
CSV files smaller than 1 GB, we will not face this problem. However, larger CSV files in
data enhancement consume resources more heavily and take more time for, population.
Therefore, the valorization times of these huge objects are significantly reduced in Dask,
which also arranges its data structures in a distributed manner, so that the divided portions
can be processed in parallel.
```
A related concept is that of the task graph . These graphs are generated before
```

computing and describe how it will be done within a system or a single machine. Graphs
represent the kind of execution path that the task scheduler will have to follow. Task
graphs are dynamic and change according to the system used. They optimize parallel
computing as much as possible.
```
You can view these graphs while computing in the Jupyter Notebook. For example, if
```

we want to see the task graph of averaging on the Dask Array considered previously, we can
write:
```
mm.dask
The list of layers into which the task graph is divided is shown in the following figure (
```

Figure 8.13 ):
```
Figure 8.13: Layers in the Task Graph
Meanwhile, if we want to see the task graph, we write:
mm.visualize()

```

Low-Level Interfacing with Dask
Delayed

The methods provided by the Pandas and NumPy libraries which were then reproduced in
the corresponding collections in Dask, can also be observed in the new methods applied to
the code. But how can we extend these new methods to parallel computing with Dask, if
they have not been implemented within it?
```
In this regard, Dask has a tool called Dask Delayed , which allows you to wrap indi-
```

vidual functions by assigning them a task graph. These functions will be incorporated
into the low-level lazily construction mechanism and will enter the same behavior as the
methods and collections of Dask.
```
Practically speaking, the functions will be defined by a @dask.delayed decorator.
```

For example, when defining a function that acts on the Dask Array and doubling all its
elements, we will anticipate the following from the decorator:
```
import dask
@dask.delayed
def doubled(x):
return 2*x
Therefore, if we now invoke this function, we will obtain a Dask Delayed object:
doubled(darr)
Delayed('doubled-5f08d4cc-aaeb-43bb-9577-7c8f055af1fd')
So, to perform the calculation of the function in parallel, we first invoke it by assigning
```

the Dask Delayed to a variable and then launching the compute() method on it:
```
d = doubled(darr)
d.compute()
A matrix with doubled elements executed in parallel by four different tasks is thus ob-
```

tained:
```
array([[ 4, 14, 6, 2, 6, 16, 2, 18, 0, 0],
[ 0, 16, 0, 12, 6, 14, 14, 6, 8, 10],
[ 0, 2, 4, 16, 12, 8, 6, 16, 10, 12],
[ 2, 16, 8, 14, 16, 4, 8, 10, 2, 16],
[ 8, 12, 8, 10, 10, 14, 8, 6, 16, 4],
[16, 10, 6, 6, 18, 8, 10, 8, 4, 10],

631
```

Begin Programming the Cluster

Everything should be ready and configured to start programming. Open a new Jupyter
Notebook on the Jupyter server and import the following modules:
```
from dask_saturn import SaturnCluster
from distributed import Client
cluster = SaturnCluster()
client = Client(cluster)
client
As we can see, these were not present in our single-machine system . To work in a
```

cluster, it is necessary to import specific modules of the cluster environment on which you
are working. However, they are provided by the host system already. Then, import
the SaturnCluster class from the dask_saturn module and launch a cluster
instance. To make Dask understand that you are not working on a single machine (default
situation), you must also instantiate a client provided by the distributed module.
We are finally ready to import the libraries for data analysis. They are practically the
same that are used in single-machine systems and look like as follows:
```
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd
In the previous section, we uploaded the prices.csv file to the Jupyter Server.
```

But the work is not yet complete. Our system includes five different machines, each with
its own memory. It is therefore necessary to add the data synchronization code between
the Jupyter Server and the workers to make data accessible for all machines. You can do
this through the following:
```
from dask_saturn import RegisterFiles, sync_files
client.register_worker_plugin(RegisterFiles())
sync_files(client, 'data')
This way, all datasets imported into the Jupyter Server data folder will be accessible to
```

all the machines in the cluster. While running this cell in Jupyter Notebook, you will notice
that the operation will take several minutes to complete. At the end of the execution, you
will get the situation of the file system after it is synchronized between all the machines in
the cluster. The following command shows this:
```
./
./prices.csv
```

Advanced Performance Optimization
Strategies with Dask

Now that we have seen how to monitor in detail the performance of individual Dask components through the dashboard and a reporting system, we can formulate a series of strategies to optimize them. Dask offers many features for parallel computing on clusters and
multi-core systems, but obtaining maximum performance requires targeted optimization,
especially for large datasets and complex tasks. This section will explore some advanced
strategies to optimize the efficiency of Dask in production environments, while paying attention to each level of operability and focusing on the configuration of the various components
involved. Some of these strategies are:

• Memory Optimization
• Data Persistence and Cache
• Data Chunk Size
• Task Merging
• Configuring Workers and Their Threads
• Configuring the Task Queue

```
Memory optimization is essential to keep Dask performing, especially while process-
```

ing large data. Efficient memory management reduces the risk of overload and makes
task completion faster. For example, by applying filter and data reduction operations
in advance, and eliminating data that is not necessary for calculation, you can reduce the
memory footprint. In this sense, it will be sufficient to apply the classic operations that
are performed with the Pandas library like column selections ( df[['col1', 'col2']]
) and data filter applications (for example, df[df['col'] > value] ) to limit the
size of the dataset. Another technique to reduce memory consumption is with data typing,
which reduces the size of variables by appropriately typing columns (for example, converting float64 to float32 ). This can significantly reduce memory usage.
```
import dask
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
n_rows = 10_000_000
```

Another important approach in the optimization process is the manual use of Garbage
Collection. Dask does not automatically initiate garbage collection between tasks. You
can force garbage collection manually with gc.collect() between intensive tasks,
which will free up unused memory.

```
Data persistence and cache is another strategy that can be applied to increase the
```

performance of distributed computing in systems like Dask. This allows us to avoid data
recalculation and improve the responsiveness of the pipeline. In this regard, the persist()
```
function allows you to keep the results of a task in memory, while avoiding recalculation
```

when these are reused in subsequent tasks. This practice is instrumental for frequently
used intermediate data. To understand this strategy, let us see another example:
```
import dask
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import time
n_rows = 10_000_000
data = {
'id': np.arange(n_rows),
'value': np.random.random(n_rows)* 100,
'category_column': np.random.choice(['A','B','C','D'], n_rows)
}
pandas_df = pd.DataFrame(data)
dask_df = dd.from_pandas(pandas_df, npartitions=10)
# Without persist()
start_time = time.time()
filtered_df = dask_df[dask_df['value']>50]
mean_without_persist = filtered_df['value'].mean().compute()
count_without_persist = filtered_df['value'].count().compute()
end_time = time.time()
time_without_persist = end_time - start_time
print(f"Mean without persist(): {mean_without_persist}")
print(f"Count without persist(): {count_without_persist}")
print(f"Time without persist(): {time_without_persist}")
```


<a id='p662'></a>
<!-- Página 662 -->


## 662 ADVANCED PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION STRATEGIES WITH DASK


```
# With persist()
start_time = time.time()
persisted_df = filtered_df.persist()
mean_with_persist = persisted_df['value'].mean().compute()
count_with_persist = persisted_df['value'].count().compute()
end_time = time.time()
time_with_persist = end_time - start_time
print(f"Mean with persist(): {mean_with_persist}")
print(f"Count with persist(): {count_with_persist}")
print(f"Time with persist(): {time_with_persist}")
print(f"Number of partitions after persist(): {persisted_df.npartitions}")

In this example, we will generate a synthetic dataset with 10 million rows. The columns
```

will include a numeric ID ( int ), a random value ( float ), and a category (
string ). When switching from Pandas to Dask, the DataFrame will be divided into 10
partitions to take leverage parallelism of the distributed system. First, we apply a complex
operation without using persist: we filter the rows where the value exceeds 50 and
calculate their average. With this type of processing, at each calculation, we will reload
the data and construct the partitions again. Then, we will perform the same operations,
this time via the persist method. In this case, the subsequent operations ( mean and
count ) are performed directly on the dataset that are already loaded into memory.
Doing so helps us avoid recalculations and improves performance. By running this code,
we will obtain a result that meets expectations and is faster at performing the operations
on the dataset where persist is used.
```
Mean without persist(): 74.9972018740045
Count without persist(): 5001671
Time without persist(): 1.0948090553283691
Mean with persist(): 74.9972018740045
Count with persist(): 5001671
Time with persist(): 0.6098389625549316
Number of partitions after persist(): 10
Here, we see that Dask demonstrates lazy behavior while executing. Therefore, we
```

will use the compute() function only when it is absolutely necessary. If used too
frequently, the task optimization features are lost. Dask performs the computation in a
lazy way and builds a task graph to optimize the execution order. By calling compute()
too early, not only will we lose the optimization aspect, but might also risk overloading the
system since this process consumes resources in its own way. Another strategy can be
enacted at the level of data subdivision and distribution. Determining the optimal size
data chunk balances memory use and computation efficiency. Chunks that are too small
can increase the system overhead, while chunks that are too large could slow down tasks.
As a rule, chunks of around 100 MB represent a good balance, but it is important to alter
their size based on the specific workload.

```
Workers can also be configured and managed optimally. A proper configuration
```

of workers based on system resources reduces execution times and improves the overall
efficiency of the cluster. The same goes for the number of threads per worker . When
optimizing, a good strategy will be to configure nthreads per worker and balance the
number of CPUs and the memory available for each worker. For example, on a system with

A particular attention in the optimization phase will be to study the configuration of
the task queue . Several bottlenecks can emerge here, which, despite the optimizations

maximum length of the queue to ensure that workers do not remain inactive.
So far, we have illustrated the most evident and essential strategies that act on the different components of the distributed system by modifying their configuration through code.
However, other unrelated factors can come into play, as they are often connected to other
technologies. In distributed clusters, the latency of communication between nodes can become a significant bottleneck and necessitates acting in a circumstantial and defined manner in the cases and architectures used. In such cases, we can try limiting communication
between workers as much as possible with technologies that compress the exchanged data
and optimize the network. It is clear that these paths require knowledge and access to
systems that often go beyond that of the programmer or the data scientist responsible for
the calculation.

GPU Parallelization in Dask:
Dask-CUDA and RAPIDS Ecosystem
(Only Linux)

We have already seen that GPUs play a key role in intensive computation, thanks to their
highly scalable parallel architecture. Dask, as an extremely powerful and versatile distributed system, supports GPU parallelization, which allows you to leverage the power of
GPUs and accelerate data science operations on large datasets. This can be a great choice
for computationally intensive applications such as ML training, large matrix computation,
and extremely complex data processing. Dask’s ability to integrate GPU processing allows you to scale your applications across multi-GPU infrastructures and distributed GPU
clusters with supported libraries such as:

• CuPy : A library for numerical computation on GPUs that replicates the NumPy API
```
and allows operations to be performed on large arrays
```

• RAPIDS and cuDF : A DataFrame management library that replicates the Pandas
```
API and is optimized for GPU processing
```

• PyTorch and TensorFlow : Dask allows you to distribute ML tasks on GPUs using
```
libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow for distributed training and inference.

To integrate GPUs in the Dask distributed computing system, the Dask-CUDA has been
```

implemented. This is an extension of Dask designed to integrate GPUs in local or distributed clusters by providing specific tools to configure clusters that automatically balance
the load between multiple GPUs on one or more nodes. More specifically, the GPU load
is managed automatically by distributing resources to balance tasks between the available
cards. It also uses CUDA Unified Memory to manage datasets that exceed the available
GPU memory. Another important feature is its ability to use GPU-specific libraries such as
cuDF, cuML and cuGraph to speed up operations similar to those performed by Pandas and
Scikit-learn on non-distributed systems. Furthermore, thanks to Dask being a distributed
computing system, Dask-CUDA can facilitate the configuration, and use of GPU clusters on
multiple machines.
```
RAPIDS is an ecosystem of GPU-accelerated libraries that offer tools similar to Pandas
```

(cuDF), NumPy (cuPy), Scikit-learn (cuML), and more. Dask can integrate seamlessly with

```
667
```

<!-- Página 668 -->

```
This program first creates a dataset with a value column containing random numbers
```

between 0 and 200, and a second category column that contains 4 random categories (A, B,
C, D). The data is converted into a cuDF DataFrame, which is managed directly on a GPU.
Then the DataFrame is split into 10 partitions and becomes a Dask-cudf Dataframe which
allows for possible distributed processing between different GPUs. A filter is applied for
rows with a value greater than 100. Finally, the computation is made effective by calling
compute (lazy behavior).
```
Let us now talk about cuPy which is the equivalent of NumPy and extends its functional-
```

ity directly to the GPUs. Here is a case where we can extend a Dask-Array to parallel GPU
computation:
```
import dask.array as da
import cupy
x = da.random.random((10000,10000), chunks=(10000,10000)).map_blocks(cupy.asarr

y = x.dot(x.T)
result = y.compute()
print(result)
```

```
})
G = cugraph.Graph()
G.from_cudf_edgelist(edges, source='src', destination='dst')
pagerank = cugraph.pagerank(G)
print("Top 5 customers: ")
print(pagerank.sort_values('pagerank', ascending=False).head(5))
```

Artificial Intelligence (AI)

A recent field of development involving computers and data analysis is Artificial Intelligence ( AI ). Through this term, we generally refer to systems / machines , which
somehow manage to imitate human intelligence. These systems, often composed of various very complex algorithms, are able to continuously improve themselves while carrying
out a given activity, thanks to the learning processes that gain experience on the basis of
the information collected. The more information they collect, the better their performance
will be.
```
Although AI is always associated with images of robots similar to human beings, it
```

is a different reality. Today, AI systems are quite widespread and operate in different
forms in our daily lives. They are incorporeal, abstract entities that manifest themselves
in different ways from the common image of humanoids. More commonly, they manage
search engines or operate behind social networks and other service distributors to study our
habits, our tastes, and our needs. These systems study our past choices and reconstruct
what our future needs could be on the basis of the information collected. For instance, it
might be projecting recommendations of a series, films on YouTube, or topics in which we
might be interested. Their purpose is to operate on the basis of the user’s choice, without
wasting time assessing thousands of possible choices.
```
Another recent application of AI are chatbots . These chats, often present on web-
```

sites of service providers, collect requests for information or ask the customers about the
problems encountered. After collecting information, they suggest the shortest way to obtain a solution such as suggesting the completion of a form, a phone number of a specific
employee, or some steps to solve the problem without having to visit a service centre.
These chatbots aim to replace a human operator by offering customer services 24 X7 .
```
On the other hand, the more profound use of AI is less evident than that of learning
```

through parameterizable model systems. This happens when AI uses large amounts of
incoming data to become accurate, which enables it to predict complex phenomena. This
approach has given rise to disciplines such as Machine Learning (ML) and Deep
Learning (DL) .

Supervised and Unsupervised
Learning

Once the areas of learning within AI have been defined, it is important to introduce another
fundamental concept before talking about their application in parallel computing.
All learning techniques, both ML and DL can follow two different approaches in the
learning phase:

• Supervised Learning
• Unsupervised Learning

These two approaches differ on whether the data used is labeled or not. By labeled
, we mean that the data is tagged with the correct answer or not .
```
Supervised learning uses data labeled with the correct answers to train models.
```

Knowing the correct answer will be used to refine the model’s capabilities in its predictions.
This approach is used in two particular techniques:

• Classification
• Regression

Classification uses algorithms to classify the data under study. Some of the most
used algorithms are:

• Logistic Regression
• K-Nearest Neighbors
• Random Forest
• Naïve Bayes
• Stochastic Gradient Descent
• Decision Trees

```
Regression instead uses algorithms that measure the relationship between a depen-
```

dent variable and one or more independent variables . Some of the more famous ones
include:

• Ridge Regression
• Lasso

```
693
```


<a id='p694'></a>
<!-- Página 694 -->

694 SUPERVISED AND UNSUPERVISED LEARNING

• Neural Network Regression
• Logistic Regression

```
In unsupervised learning , the data comes without explicit labels. Therefore, such
```

algorithms can work without human supervision. While this approach is valuable, most
state-of-the-art DL applications such as image classification and NLP rely on supervised or
self-supervised learning, rather than purely unsupervised methods.
```
There are three different techniques that follow this approach:

```

• Clustering
• Association
• Dimensionality Reduction

```
Clustering is based on the similarities or differences of the data under study by group-
```

ing them according to certain characteristics. The best-known algorithm that follows this
technique is K-means clustering .
```
Association can identify the relationship between the variables within a dataset.
```

Relationships are not yet defined before studying the dataset.
```
Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of features to be studied within a
```

dataset that can sometimes be too large. Algorithms that follow this technique must be
able to reduce the number of features that distinguish the data, without compromising their
integrity.

Artificial Intelligence and Parallel
Computing

As we can certainly guess, the creation of complex computer systems capable of carrying out
forms of AI requires enormous computing resources. As their capabilities grow, more powerful computers will be required. This is why these AI systems have become widespread
only in the recent years. It is therefore clear that in order to be able to operate in this
sector and develop AI systems that are capable of carrying out their tasks, we will have to
leverage systems based on parallel computing, as they are the only ones that can provide
the necessary computing resources.
```
Clouds, for example, have abundant computational power that allow operators and de-
```

velopers to obtain high-performance computational power at affordable prices. Prior to
this development, the only computing environments available for AI had to work on a small
set of cost-prohibitive supercomputers. If you would have worked on single computers,
you could have only create simple models with long processing times, which in any case
would require the additional support of different GPU cards to operate. It is therefore
clear that the latter case can be a choice for a study or development environment.





Parallel and Distributed Machine
Learning

As far as ML is concerned, Python offers ample opportunities as it is a popular reference language for this discipline. There are many libraries available that provide ML algorithms,
such as:

• scikit-learn
• XGBoost
• LightGBM
• TensorFlow

```
Furthermore, many of these libraries are designed to operate on parallel systems ( par-
```

allel computing ). They can also be extended in environments formed by multiple machines ( distributed computing ). This is precisely due to the fact that ML requires a lot
of computing resources and therefore it is natural to use it on powerful systems capable
of parallel computing.
```
For ML, we need to carry out operations for which the parallel computing approach is
```

fundamental. The most important of these is matrix multiplication . We have already
seen in the first few chapters of the book that it can greatly benefit from correct parallel
implementation, especially if GPUs are used to perform this calculation. Multiplication
between matrices is the basis of linear regression algorithms that are widely used in ML.
Reducing the time taken in this type of calculation clearly affects the general performance
of the learning phases and the calculation of the predictions made by ML models.
```
Another common operation in ML is calculating the distance between two points .
```

This operation is common in many algorithms (such as k-means clustering ) and is
performed many times within the same algorithm. Since they take advantage of the fact
that the individual distance calculation of subsequent iterations does not depend on other
calculations in the same iteration, these calculations can be performed in parallel to reduce
processing times.
```
Also, in the context of operations that could be onerous in terms of ML execution, there
```

exists k-fold cross-validation , which is based on the intense processing of different
segments of the dataset. This method is used to validate a model and is based on excluding
one of the k segments (fold) from the calculation. All other k-1 segments are trained and

```
697
```


<a id='p698'></a>
<!-- Página 698 -->


## 698 PARALLEL AND DISTRIBUTED MACHINE LEARNING


then the k-th element is used as a test dataset. Since we are dealing with k segments, this
operation is performed k times , each of which excludes a different segment from training.
Once k results are obtained, their average is calculated. As can be understood, the
k-fold cross-validation algorithm, if performed sequentially, takes a large amount of time
as it has to repeat the same operations k times. If it is brought in parallel form, where each
calculation performed on one of the k folds is performed simultaneously, we can observe
significant gains in performance.
```
All these operations, if processed in a parallel computing system, can ML much more
```

efficient and capable of tackling more complex problems. ML can then also process larger
datasets and increase the forecasting capacity of the models, while also reducing processing
times. These features can otherwise become prohibitive in a single machine system.

<a id='p699'></a>
<!-- Página 699 -->

Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn

Scikit-learn is currently the most used Python library in Machine Learning and provides
users with main algorithms such as:

• Classification
• Clustering

• Dimensionality Reduction

```
Scikit-learn is a well-documented library with several available examples. To know
```

how ML works with scikit-learn , let us look at a simple example of linear regression .
Among the various examples, this one is simple to understand and is the perfect illustrative
case even for people who are not familiar with ML. This technique is based on the construction of a very simple model of a system that is supposed to behave linearly, in order to
predict the result from a given value of a variable in this system.
```
For simplicity, we will use data points generated around a straight line that distances
```

them by a random value from the correct linear trend. In this way, we can simulate the
data coming from a phenomenon that responds to a linear behavior from which we will
have to obtain the linear trend (intercept and coefficient of the slope of the straight line).
To do this, we generate a dataset of 30 values from the equation of a straight line with
slope 0.3 and coefficient 1.0, to which we add a random noise that simulates
the deviation of the values from the correct trend.
```
import numpy as np
x = 50 * np.random.random((30, 1))
y = 0.3 * x + 1.0 + np.random.normal(size=x.shape)
Once the dataset(x,y) has been generated, in which x will be the variables
```

and y will represent the labels with the results, we can divide it into two parts.
We will use one of these as a training set and the other as a testing set . We can do
this via a convenient function provided by scikit-learn called train_test_split(),
which allows us to split a dataset based on a percentage defined by the test_size
parameter. So, if we want 20% of the dataset for testing, we will write the following
code:
```
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2)
```

generated, we will move on to the learning phase, using the fit() method and passing

```
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
```

Scaling Scikit-learn with Dask-ML

Just like what we saw in the previous chapter , Dask can be an excellent solution for scaling
ML applications in distributed environments. Like Dask DataFrames for Pandas and
Dask Arrays for NumPy , the Dask-ML module extends the scikit-learn library on
distributed environments such as clusters.
```
This module takes advantage of one of scikit-learn’s parallel computing features:
```

joblib . Many scikit-learn algorithms have been implemented to run in parallel when
using joblib , which provides thread-based and process-based parallelism natively. Dask-ML will use this capability to distribute these computations across a cluster.
This same mechanism is also used to implement machine learning models of other libraries
like XGboost .
```
To install Dask-ML in a virtual environment specifically created for ML, follow the
```

given steps:

1. Open a command shell and enter the following command:
```
conda install dask-ml -c conda-forge
conda install joblib
conda install matplotlib -c conda-forge

```

2. Once the installation is complete, we will open a notebook on Jupyter via:
```
from dask.distributed import Client
client = Client()

```

3. Dask-ML , similar to Dask, provides a set of methods and functions corresponding to
```
the original libraries. However, they can work only on distributed environments.
In this case, the train_test_split() function of scikit-learn will be replaced
with the same function of the Dask-ML library, which is shown here:
from dask_ml.model_selection import train_test_split
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2)

```

4. Like the scikit-learn functions, the models are also provided in their own version dis-
```
tributed by Dask-ML. Let us replace the LinearRegression class of scikit-learn
with that of Dask-ML. At this point, the learning methods fit() and evaluation
predict() will be \provided by Dask-ML for distributed environments.

703
```


<a id='p704'></a>
<!-- Página 704 -->

704

```
from dask_ml.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression()
Before moving on to the learning phase, we need to add the joblib library.
This particular library allows Python libraries like scikit-learn to work in parallel on a
single machine. With parallel_backend provided by this library, it is possible
to do it by taking into account the features of Dask. In this way, we can execute the
code in parallel computing mode even in a distributed environment , which enhance
the library’s performance even more.
import joblib
from joblib import parallel_backend
with parallel_backend('dask'):
model.fit(x_train,y_train)
y_new = model.predict(x_test)

```

5. Now that we have trained and evaluated the model in parallel, we can check the results
```
graphical via:
```

Parallel and Distributed Deep
Learning

At the base of DL are neural networks, which are excellent for discovering the relationships
and structures that are hidden behind unsupervised data. Their ability to learn and
analyze , which in emulates the human way of learning, makes them suitable for working
on data that is not strictly numerical in nature, such as images and sounds. This is why DL
is particularly focused on Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision .
```
Artificial neural networks are complex structures that require huge computing resources
```

to operate efficiently. The typical neural networks used in DL use millions of parameters
that make up a model. These systems also take the advantage of a large amount of data for
their learning. Therefore, this process is computationally intensive and will take an enormous amount of time in single-machine systems . Furthermore, many datasets are too
large to be contained within the memory of a single machine. Fortunately, the particular
layered structure of neurons in a neural network is perfectly suited to distributed systems
and allows you to make the most of parallel computing. The models used for DL can be
distributed over the different layers of the neural network, and its parameters (weights) are
in turn distributed among the different neurons present in each layer. So, it is clear that
we can use these features to distribute the load and information of the models used, as well
as their relative calculation on different machines in a distributed system.
```
There are several methods to distribute and thereby parallelize computation when train-
```

ing on clusters of machines. These methods can be used singularly or in combination.

• Parallel Processing

```
– Multi-Core Processing
– GPU Processing

```

• Distributed Training

```
– Data Parallelism
– Model Parallelism

Through these methods, it will be possible to convert DL algorithms into parallel algo-
```

rithms, where single tasks will be assigned to the different cores (multi-core processing), or
to the different GPUs present on the machines (GPUs processing). As for datasets, since

```
707
```


<a id='p708'></a>
<!-- Página 708 -->

708 PARALLEL AND DISTRIBUTED DEEP LEARNING

they tend to be enormous in size, they can be divided and distributed on different machines
( data parallelism) to reduce memory overloads. Even DL models can be divided into
smaller parts, while assigning a set of parameters for each machine ( model parallelism
). Both of these methods can reduce learning time significantly. However, data parallelism is often preferred over model parallelism . In fact, in the latter case, there
are synchronization operations that require more processing time. Therefore, data parallelism is the fastest approach between the two . On the other hand, model parallelism
produces better predictive results.

<a id='p709'></a>
<!-- Página 709 -->

PyTorch and TensorFlow

Among the various possibilities offered by Python to work with DL, there are two opensource frameworks that have been very popular lately:

• PyTorch
• TensorFlow

```
PyTorch is a relatively new DL framework. This library was developed by the
```

Facebook AI Lab and was released as open-source on GitHub in 2017 . Its main
purpose was to implement applications for Natural Language Processing ( NLP ).
PyTorch soon gained success for its simplicity, efficient use of memory, and being largely
native as it produced code with higher processing speed.
```
TensorFlow is also an open-source framework built specifically for DL. This library
```

was developed by Google and first released in 2015 . Compared to PyTorch, TensorFlow is more popular . This is because it has been present for longer and has a large
amount of documentation available. It also has abundant support from other technologies
that facilitate scalability on distributed systems and on different platforms like Android
. Furthermore, since 2017 , TensorFlow has integrated Keras , which is another DL
framework that has existed for several years. TensorFlow is currently the preferred tool
for many professionals and researchers and is used to train several models.




```

class FashionCNN(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
```

```
super(FashionCNN, self).__init__()
self.layer1 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),

nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)
)
self.layer2 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=32, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3),
nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(2)
)
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=64*6*6, out_features=600)
self.drop = nn.Dropout2d(0.25)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=600, out_features=120)
self.fc3 = nn.Linear(in_features=120, out_features=10)
def forward(self, x):
out = self.layer1(x)
out = self.layer2(out)
out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
out = self.fc1(out)
out = self.drop(out)
out = self.fc2(out)
out = self.fc3(out)
return out
```

Once both the datasets and the neural network model are ready, we can move on to
implementing the model learning phases, and simultaneously calculating the model’s accuracy and loss during the learning phase. These values will be useful later to evaluate
the goodness of the model obtained.
```
def train(bs, lr):
batch_size = bs
learning_rate = lr
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(training_data,batch_size)

test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(test_data,batch_size)
#device = torch.device('cuda:0')
device = torch.device('cpu')
num_epochs = 5
count = 0
model = FashionCNN()
```


<a id='p721'></a>
<!-- Página 721 -->

```
721

model.to(device)
error = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
learning_rate = 0.001
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
training_start_time = datetime.datetime.now()
results = []
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
for images, labels in train_loader:
images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
train = Variable(images.view(100, 1, 28, 28))
outputs = model(train)
loss = error(outputs, labels)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
count += 1
# Testing the model
if not (count % 50): # It's same as "if count % 50 == 0"
total = 0
correct = 0
for images, labels in test_loader:
images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
test = Variable(images.view(100, 1, 28, 28))
outputs = model(test)
predictions = torch.max(outputs, 1)[1].to(device)
correct += (predictions == labels).sum()
total += len(labels)

accuracy = correct * 100 / total
new_results = {
"batch_size": batch_size,
"loss": loss.data.item(),
"iteration": count,
"accuracy": accuracy.item(),
"elapsed_time_sec": (datetime.datetime.now() - training_start_time).total_secon

}
results.append(new_results)
return results
```

To visualize the graphic scheme of the neural network defined with PyTorch, or to get detailed information on the structure we are using, you can use the following tools:

```
735

The graph generated with torchviz represents the dynamic computational graph of the
```

FashionCNN neural network, which describes how tensors are transformed and passed
through the various layers of the model to produce the output. The nodes represent an
operation (for example, Convolution, ReLU, pooling, linear operations) or a transformation
applied to the tensors. Each node is depicted as a rectangle labeled with the name of the related operation. The edges of the graph instead represent the flow of tensors in the model,
showing how one operation feeds the next. Each connection represents an intermediate
tensor. As for the nodes, these are represented with two colors. The main nodes are
colored blue or purple and represent the operations explicitly defined in the model, while
the gray ones are the intermediate nodes, and represent the intermediate tensors created
during the forward pass.
```
Torchviz is therefore a useful tool to understand the functioning of complex models and
```

to diagnose problems in the construction of the graph.
```
A different functionality is offered by torchsummary and torchinfo .
```

define an ad hoc function, but it is sufficient to call the summary method provided by both

```
Finally, another tool available online is Netron , which accepts different model
```

formats, including torchScript . Just like torchviz , Netron is a

its interactive nature, it allows you to obtain detailed information for each element of the
network (nodes and connections) by clicking on them, as well as zooming in to focus the
study on particular sections of the model.

```
To convert our model into this format, we can use the following code:
def save_model_for_netron(model):
model.eval()
example_input = torch.randn(1, 1, 28, 28)
traced_model = torch.jit.trace(model, example_input)
traced_model.save("FashionCNN.pt")
print("Saved model as FashionCNN.pt")
model = FashionCNN()
save_model_for_netron(model)
Go to the Netron web page ( https://netron.app/ ) and upload the file you just generated.
```

```
class FashionCNN(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
super(FashionCNN, self).__init__()
self.layer1 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),

nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)
)
```


<a id='p746'></a>
<!-- Página 746 -->

746 SCALING PYTORCH WITH DASK

```
self.layer2 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=32, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3),
nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(2)
)
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=64*6*6, out_features=600)
self.drop = nn.Dropout2d(0.25)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=600, out_features=120)
self.fc3 = nn.Linear(in_features=120, out_features=10)
def forward(self, x):
out = self.layer1(x)
out = self.layer2(out)
out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
out = self.fc1(out)
out = self.drop(out)
out = self.fc2(out)
out = self.fc3(out)
return out
```

Now, we need to insert the neural network training code that we enclosed in a train()
function. Doing this facilitates the integration of this code with Dask. The Dask library
provides a @dask.delayed decorator that allows you to distribute the code enclosed
within the function to which it is related in different tasks. These will be then assigned to
many workers who will execute them in parallel. The only concern for the developer is to
add the decorator, which they can do via:
```
@dask.delayed
def train(bs, lr):
batch_size = bs
learning_rate = lr
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(training_data,batch_size)

test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(test_data,batch_size)
device = torch.device('cuda:0')
num_epochs = 5
count = 0
model = FashionCNN()
model.to(device)
error = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
training_start_time = datetime.datetime.now()
results = []
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
```


<a id='p747'></a>
<!-- Página 747 -->

```
747

for images, labels in train_loader:
images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
train = Variable(images.view(100, 1, 28, 28))
labels = Variable(labels)
outputs = model(train)
loss = error(outputs, labels)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
count += 1
# Testing the model
if not (count % 50):
total = 0
correct = 0
for images, labels in test_loader:
images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
test = Variable(images.view(100, 1, 28, 28))
outputs = model(test)
predictions = torch.max(outputs, 1)[1].to(device)
correct += (predictions == labels).sum()
total += len(labels)

accuracy = correct * 100 / total
new_results = {
"batch_size": batch_size,
"loss": loss.data.item(),
"iteration": count,
"accuracy": accuracy.item(),
"elapsed_time_sec": (datetime.datetime.now() - training_start_time).total_secon

}
results.append(new_results)
return results
```

```
train_future = client.map(train, experiment)
```

Massively Parallel Artificial
Intelligence

Among the innovations in AI, the most imminent one is the development of Massively
Parallel Artificial Intelligence , which is based on the increasing availability of massively
parallel systems (see Figure 10.1 ).
Figure 10.1: Massively Parallel System Model
```
The term, Massively Parallel System refers to a set of many processing units structured
```

to carry out a certain operation by working in parallel.
These systems have existed before the 1970s and have evolved through technological innovations. Generally, we can identify these systems as linked to a particular type of supercomputer, where the processing units such as CPUs, GPUs, or separate machines (massively
parallel machines) are arranged in parallel and perform a specific portion of a task.
Today, massively parallel systems are growing to be increasingly powerful. Facebook
and Google are among the major users of these systems, as the latter are capable of managing immense amounts of data that arrives from search engines and social networks.
```
The particular parallel structure, made up of homogeneous and independent units, also
```

allows these systems to be scaled according to calculation needs.
For example, if one of these systems requires more resources to keep up with applications, extra processing units can easily be added to the system, wherever necessary. If,
on the other hand, the computing resources are excessive, they could be deactivated or allocated to other tasks, which prevents wastage of resources.
The nature of these particular systems, as well as their increasing power and flexibility,
makes them suitable for the use of AI. The same AI is then used for to tune its own performance. This allows these systems to adapt dynamically in an autonomous and efficient
way to cater to various calculation needs.
This new area of AI research possesses unimaginable computing power which will result
into better and large scale computing performance. However, this is not the goal of such
systems. As we have seen before, with the transition from Machine Learning (ML) to
Deep Learning (DL), this computing power will certainly lead to the emergence of a new
approach towards the creation of intelligent systems. For example, new methods are being
developed to introduce forms of memory-based reasoning into applications. Another
technique that has been in vogue is parallel marker passing , with which new highly

and policy systems and will gradually have to be integrated into data processing with the

and build a solid foundation of reasoning.

Distributed Computing
Infrastructure with Cyber-Physical
Systems

The previous section immediately brings to mind other disciplines and related technologies
that are involved with the innovation of AI and the integration of increasingly intelligent
systems in our society.
We talked about data sources, future edge computing, and the growing use of sensors
and other forms of real-world data capture. Technological advances in communication
technologies and the possibility of coverage by Wi-Fi systems have led to the birth and development of the Internet of Things ( IoT ). Cyber-Physical Systems ( CPS ) play a
decisive role in this new “ distributed ” data acquisition system.
These are computer systems whose purpose is to interact continuously with the real environment in which they operate. CPS systems therefore must meet three fundamental
requirements to be considered as such:

• Computing
• Communication
• Control

Systems equipped with these three properties collect data through a network of sensors
or other human interfaces, process them in an increasingly intelligent way, and communicate the processed information with other computer systems connected to them (edge
computing). Figure 10.3 shows the evolution of the scheme represented in Figure 10.2
with the introduction of Cyber-Physical Systems in edge computing. CPS are capable of
processing input data, extrapolating abstract information, and interacting with the external
environment via actuators or Human-Machine interfaces ( HMI ).
```
Figure 10.3: The Evolution of Edge Computing through Intelligent Systems (Cyber-
```

Physical Systems)
Furthermore, this Cyber-Physical System will also be able to control the physical environment in which it operates through actuators or other physical interaction systems,
based on the information processed or received. The future goal is to make these systems increasingly intelligent, while integrating them with applications capable of learning,

activities. Entrusting all these operations and visibility to controlled intelligent systems
requires a corresponding development of new security systems.

```
This reality is not that distant. Recent studies show that AI has already taken over
```

many fields, some of which are sensitive enough to impact integral matters such as privacy
and security. Sectors such as finance, military, transportation, and hospitals already use
AI, with more applications yet to come in the next few years. Their intrusion of antisocial and criminal elements that misuse AI can wreck devastating damage on the society.
It therefore necessitates the development of security systems capable of exerting control
