Another emerging trend in technological innovations is Exascale computing . The term
indicates a new level of supercomputing that is capable of performing at least 1,000,000,000,000,000,000
floating point operations per second (Exaflops). Such computing power can increase the
performance of applications that use parallel computing.

Quantum Computing

Parallel computing is destined to evolve with the birth of new computing technologies that
are completely different from the earlier versions. One of these is Quantum Computing
. This computing system bases its operation on the quantum properties of matter, such as
the superposition of states and entanglement. Thanks to these properties, these systems
are able to perform operations on data on quantum bits instead of transistors that operate
in binary state (0 or 1). Quantum bits are also called qubits and are capable of processing
multiple values simultaneously, which completely distorts the basics of the binary code.
```
Computers based on quantum computing are already intrinsically parallel at a very low
```

level. These characteristics promise upheavals in computing performance. It is clear
that these technologies require an upheaval of parallel computing basics, which gives birth
to new concepts and approaches.
```
The potential of quantum computers has led to a real race among various nations of the
```

world to create such systems. Although the technology is fresh, these computers already
exist and new versions are being created. The first quantum computer was marketed by
IBM in 2019 and is called IBM Q System One . Subsequently, the US created a series of
quantum computers called Eagle (127 qubits) in the form of chips that can be adapted to
the new system: IBM System Two and its corresponding software.
```
In Canada, Xanadu has joined the superpowers with the creation of a quantum computer
```

based on photon entanglement, which is called Borealis (216 qubits). This system was
used to calculate the Gaussian boson sampling of 216 photons in just 36 microseconds.
Such a problem would have required over 9,000 years of computation on today’s fastest
supercomputers.
```
As far as Europe is concerned, two quantum computers are already active (Paris in
```

France, and Jülich in Germany) out of the 6 that are under construction (one of which is in
Italy) which will form the first quantum computer network in the world. These machines
will be used for research but will also be made accessible to European start-ups and companies in order to stimulate subsequent technological progress. Even more recent (2022)
is the news from China that has created its first quantum computer, Wuyan , which is
equipped with 24 qubits and is built by Origin Quantum Computing.
```
Quantum technology, when integrated with the existing HPC systems, will pave way for
```

significant advances in all sectors of the industry.

Introduction

In this chapter, we further extend the world of distributed computing by introducing another framework called Ray , while adding it to Celery and Dask as an additional tool to
handle complex computations. We take the Monte Carlo method as an example to show
how some computations can be extended from local systems to distributed systems, while
increasing performance and the ability to handle large, structured data. We also cover
extensive modules such as Ray Train , Ray Tune and Ray Serve that are specifically designed to extend Machine Learning (ML) developed with TensorFlow, PyTorch and
other frameworks in distributed environments. Finally, we introduce Modin , a library
that provides methods for computing and manipulating DataFrame objects in distributed
environments, preserving the Pandas syntax.

The Ray Framework

Ray is an open-source framework designed to simplify parallel and distributed computing
in Python, while allowing developers to scale their applications across CPU and GPU clusters
without making significant code changes. With its flexible architecture, Ray is used for a
wide range of applications, including distributed machine learning, hyperparameter tuning,
real-time inference, and reinforcement learning. With an intuitive API and advanced
modules such as Ray Tune and Ray Serve , Ray has become a must-have tool for those
looking to leverage parallel computing at scale. Ray can be installed with a simple pip
command. In a production environment, it can be deployed on clusters, Kubernetes, or
cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure via:
```
pip install ray
Once installed, Ray can be initialized with ray.init() to use a local or distributed
```

environment.
```
import ray
# Ray initialization
ray.init()
When you call ray.init() in a Python program, Ray performs a series of oper-
```

ations to set up and initialize the distributed computing environment. When Ray starts,
it starts with some components such as the Ray Head Node, which is the local instance of
the Ray runtime on your machine. This is when you would want to consider creating or
using a local cluster, but you can also specify the address of a remote cluster that is already
running, without having to start a new instance locally. If the cluster is local and has
already started, you can use:
```
ray.init(address="auto")
If the cluster you are running is remote, you need to specify the address and port as:
ray.init(address="ray://123.45.67.89:10001")
When you start a Ray instance, a dashboard also appears on the default port 8265 in
```

localhost (127.0.0.1) reachable via browser. If you are working on Jupyter Notebook, you
will be shown a window (see Figure 11.1 ), which shows the versions of Python and Ray
in use and the URL of the Ray Dashboard.
```
Figure 11.1: Notice of a Ray Instance on a Jupyter Notebook
Once Ray is instantiated, various processes are started in sequence to manage distributed
```

computing and resources. Each node (including the local one) runs a process called Raylet
(Resource Manager), which is responsible for managing the available resources (memory,

```
807
```


<a id='p808'></a>
<!-- Página 808 -->

808 THE RAY FRAMEWORK




```
Figure 152:




Figure 153:


```

CPU and GPU). These processes will be responsible for scheduling the execution of tasks
and actors based on the available resources. Another process that will be started is Redis
(which we have already seen in a previous chapter for distributed systems). Ray uses Redis
as a Metadata Store to store system information and state data of the cluster in use. Then
an Object Store (Plasma Store) will be started to manage distributed data. The objects that
will be returned by the tasks will be stored here and will be accessible to all the workers
of the cluster. Finally, Ray starts one or more worker processes that execute the remote
tasks. A general scheme of the Ray architecture and how the components are distributed
is shown in Figure 11.2 .
```
Figure 11.2: Ray Architecture
Also, when ray.init() is launched, the system will use the maximum of the avail-
```

able resources. If you want to use only a part of the resources, it will be better to specify
it by passing the number of resources to dedicate to distribute computing as parameters

<a id='p809'></a>
<!-- Página 809 -->

```
809

```

explicitly.
```
ray.init(num_cpus=4, num_gpus=1)
```

Once all the necessary calculations have been performed, it is necessary to close the
started Ray system with all its components. To do this, you must launch the command:
```
ray.shutdown()
```

This command is also useful to reset the system in development and start anew in case of
an error. To know the number of workers available with Ray, that is the number of available computing resources (if we used ray.init() without parameters), the simplest
way is to use ray.available_resources() , as demonstrated here:
```
resources = ray.available_resources()
print(f"Num of CPUs: {resources.get('CPU', 0)}")
print(f"Num of GPUs: {resources.get('GPU', 0)}")
```

By running these lines, you will get the following information about the resources available in the system:
```
Num of CPUs: 12.0
Num of GPUs: 0
```

## 810 THE RAY FRAMEWORK


<a id='p811'></a>
<!-- Página 811 -->

The Basic Components of Ray: Task
and Actor

A main feature of Ray is its ability to distribute computations easily and efficiently in an environment. Ray is able to distribute computations across multiple CPU and GPU cores both
on a single machine and in a cluster, without the need to manually manage the complexity of networking or synchronization. It also allows you to manage almost automatically
independent tasks and more complex applications with interdependent tasks.
```
The characteristics and operation of Ray can be described more quickly and comprehen-
```

sively through its architecture. The framework is based on two main components:

• Task
• Actor

```
A task is a function that is executed in parallel and in a distributed way. Tasks
```

can be executed on multiple cores or nodes in parallel: when you call a remote function,
it is executed on a remote worker (which can be on the same machine or a cluster), and
the result is returned as a future reference (‘ ObjectRef ‘). This also introduces
asynchrony since this reference can be used after the task call to retrieve the result. Ray
also has a system, called Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that tracks the dependencies between
the various tasks and thus optimizes their execution in a completely automatic way.
```
Actors distribute Python objects that maintain their own state and provide remote meth-
```

ods. Actors are useful when you need to maintain a shared state or perform successive
operations on the same distributed object. Their state is guaranteed to persist during the
sequential execution of calls and their entire lifecycle develops within a single worker.
Ray will then take care of creating multiple actor instances in cases where it will be necessary to distribute the work, by automatically scaling applications on CPU and GPU clusters,
and adapting the number of workers based on the complexity of the workload. Actors will
be particularly useful for scenarios such as:

• Data Caching
• Resource Pool Management
• Coordinating between Distributed Tasks


```
811
```


<a id='p812'></a>
<!-- Página 812 -->

812 THE BASIC COMPONENTS OF RAY: TASK AND ACTOR

```
We will approach this library for the first time by directly seeing the operation of these
```

two components through some example codes. In Ray, you can define both the functions
and the classes defined within the code respectively as Ray Task and Ray Actor using the
‘ @ray.remote ‘ decorator. Once defined, they can be used inside the code with
the suffix .remote() that tells Ray to execute on one of the workers in a distributed
manner. However, to be able to use a distributed system efficiently we must ensure that
the calculation occurs in parallel on multiple workers at the same time. Let us see an
example in which we will perform a calculation on 10 values at the same time:
```
# Define a distributed and parallel function
@ray.remote
def compute_square(x):
return x * x
# Parallel execution of tasks
futures = [compute_square.remote(i) for i in range(10)]
results = ray.get(futures)
print("Results: ", results)
Running the code generates the following result:
Results: [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]
Here, we are running the compute_square() task that calculates the square of
```

a value on 10 values (from 0 to 9) generated by the range() function. The
square.remote(i) call occurs 10 times, so 10 independent tasks will be started. The
calculation does not return the result directly, but via an ObjectRef , which is a
reference to an object that will be calculated in the future. In fact, the results are retrieved
later, through the ray.get() function that takes futures references as an argument
and returns the results calculated by the remote workers. If we run the code, we get the
expected result, that is, a list of the squares of the numbers from 0 to 9.
```
It is also possible to combine multiple remote tasks, while creating calculation pipelines,
```

as we see in the following example:
```
@ray.remote
def add(x,y):
return x + y
@ray.remote
def multiply(x, y):
return x * y
result = multiply.remote(add.remote(1, 2), 3)
print("Results: ", ray.get(result))
Executing the code fetches you the result shown here:
Results: 9
As for actors, we will explore the defined classes that have the decorator @ray.remote
```

. Here is a simple example that uses a counter:
```
@ray.remote
class Counter:
```


<a id='p813'></a>
<!-- Página 813 -->

```
813

def __init__(self):
self.count = 0
def increment(self):
self.count += 1
return self.count
counter = Counter.remote()
print(ray.get(counter.increment.remote()))
print(ray.get(counter.increment.remote()))
```

Executing the code fetches you the result shown here:
```
1
2
```

The use of a counter shows the maintenance of the internal state of an actor, which in this
case is self.count . To create a remote instance of this counter, the remote()
suffix is also used in this case. In this way, the instance is executed directly on one of
the available workers. Each actor will be assigned to a separate worker and its state will
be local. The increment method is a remote method and will be executed on the worker
where the relative actor persists. At each call, the value of the counter will be incremented
by one unit, regardless of all the other operations performed (not present in the example
code). Here too, ray.get() is used to recall the value returned by the remote
method.
The behavior of the actors and the permanence of their states become more evident, if
we instantiate two different counters:
```
counter1 = Counter.remote()
counter2 = Counter.remote()
counter1.increment.remote()
counter1.increment.remote()
futures = [counter2.increment.remote(), counter1.increment.remote()]

results = ray.get(futures)
print("Results:", results)
Running the code will fetch us this result:
Results: [1, 3]
As we can see in the code, counter 1 is incremented 3 times, while the second counter
```

is incremented only once. We can capture the results only for the final increments and
display the count values in the output.

<a id='p814'></a>
<!-- Página 814 -->


## 814 THE BASIC COMPONENTS OF RAY: TASK AND ACTOR


<a id='p815'></a>
<!-- Página 815 -->

An Example of Parallel Calculation
with the Monte Carlo Method

Let us move on to a more complex computational case such as calculating the estimate of
the value of π with the Monte Carlo method. This is a classic case already used in the book
and is perfect for demonstrating parallelism because each point generated is independent
of the others. This makes it ideal for distributed computing.
```
In this example, we generate random points (x, y) in a square of side 2 centered on the
```

origin. We then count how many of these points fall inside a circle of radius 1, which is also
centered on the origin. The fraction of points that fall inside the circle is approximately
equal to the area of the circle divided by the area of the square, or π/4, from which we can
estimate the value of π.
```
import ray
import random
@ray.remote
def monte_carlo_simulation(num_samples):
inside_circle = 0
for _ in range(num_samples):
x = random.uniform(-1, 1)
y = random.uniform(-1, 1)
if x**2 + y**2 <= 1:
inside_circle += 1
return inside_circle
def estimate_pi(total_samples, num_workers):
samples_per_worker = total_samples // num_workers
futures = [monte_carlo_simulation.remote(samples_per_worker) for _ in
```

range(num_workers)]
```
total_inside_circle = sum(ray.get(futures))
pi_estimate = 4 * (total_inside_circle / total_samples)
return pi_estimate
if __name__ == "__main__":
ray.init()
total_samples = 10_000_000

The monte_carlo_simulation function calculates the number of points falling
inside the circle for a given number of samples. This function is decorated with
@ray.remote , which means that each call to this function will be executed on a separate worker. To distribute the Monte Carlo computation load, the estimate_pi
```
function is defined, which divides the total number of samples among the number of work-
```

ers. Each worker will run the Monte Carlo simulation on a fraction of the total. Inside it,
the parallel computation will be performed through a list of futures by issuing as many
.remote() calls to the monte_carlo_simulation function as there are workers
available in Ray. The result is then retrieved by collecting the results from all the individual workers via ray.get(futures) and adding them together. Running this gives
the following result:
```
Estimate of π with 10 000 000 samples distributed in 8 workers: 3.1416712

As we can see, we have obtained an estimated value of π that differs from the original
```

(3.14159) in the fourth decimal place.
```
We can also compare the results in terms of the efficiency of the distributed computation
```

with the classical sequential one. We will introduce the measure of the time taken to
perform the Monte Carlo computation. Let us insert the appropriate measurements in the
previous code:
```
import time
if __name__ == "__main__":
total_samples = 10_000_000
num_workers = 8
start_time = time.time()
pi_estimate = estimate_pi(total_samples, num_workers)
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Estimate of π with {total_samples} samples distributed in {num_workers
```

workers: {pi_estimate}")
```
print(f"Calculated in {end_time - start_time} sec")
Running the code will fetch us this result (it can vary from system to system and from
```

the number of available workers):
```
Estimate of π with 10000000 samples distributed in 8 workers: 3.1419852

Calculated in 1.084900140762329 sec
```

Now let us write the code equivalent to the previous one for the classical sequential
computation of the estimate of π:
```
import random
```


<a id='p817'></a>
<!-- Página 817 -->

```
817

import time
def monte_carlo_pi_sequential(num_samples):
inside_circle = 0
for _ in range(num_samples):
x = random.uniform(-1, 1)
y = random.uniform(-1, 1)
if x**2 + y**2 <= 1:
inside_circle += 1
return 4 * (inside_circle / num_samples)
total_samples = 10_000_000
start_time = time.time()
pi_estimate = monte_carlo_pi_sequential(total_samples)
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Estimate of π with {total_samples} samples: {pi_estimate}")
print(f"Calculated in {end_time - start_time} sec")

Estimate of π with 10000000 samples: 3.141688
Calculated in 4.491239547729492 sec

Using Ray to Distribute AI
Applications and Machine Learning
Tasks

Ray is a versatile tool for distributing AI and ML applications across CPU and GPU clusters,
as it allows you to run complex and intensive tasks in parallel. Ray’s ability to handle asynchronous tasks and support distributed pipelines makes it particularly useful for processing
resource-intensive ML processes such as model training, hyperparameter tuning, and distributed inference. This section explores how to use Ray to distribute AI applications and
ML tasks, while analyzing best practices and some practical examples. Ray is an excellent
tool for distributing ML model training, thanks to the integration of advanced modules that
extend its functionality. These are listed as follows:

• Ray Train for distributed learning
• Ray Tune for hyperparameter optimization
• Ray Serve for distributed model serving
• Ray Rllib, which is a reinforcement learning toolkit

```
This set of libraries are specifically created to integrate with popular ML libraries such
```

as PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost, and scikit-learn, while providing scalability in distributed
systems and running experiments on multiple cores, GPUs or nodes in a cluster.
```
Note : These modules have been used in this book with PyTorch, but they can be used
```

in many other contexts. They have been implemented to work in Linux environments and
present a series of problems that require ad hoc corrections if you are working on Windows
environments (such as path names that are too long and exceed the maximum number of characters allowed, and so on.). It is advisable to work in a Linux context for this kind of study.
```
Ray Train is designed to simplify distributed training of ML models across multiple
```

machines, CPUs, GPUs, and nodes in a cluster. Distributed training takes advantage of
the parallelism between multiple machines and GPUs in a cluster, while allowing you to
use large datasets for learning in a scalable way. It can dynamically add resources during the learning process, if necessary. It also implements special techniques, such as
AllReduce , which synchronize gradients during distributed training. Finally, it is also
able to save and restore checkpoints to ensure resilience in case of errors. To integrate

```
819
```


<a id='p820'></a>
<!-- Página 820 -->

820

this library into the Ray framework, run the following command:
```
pip install -U ray[train]
This integration allows the use of trainers from existing Deep Learning systems such as
```

TorchTrainer or TensorFlowTrainer , while running them in a distributed
manner. Distributed datasets are also supported in this integration, which allow developers to manage large amounts of data during the learning phase. In addition, a monitoring
system is provided with the train.report() method that records metrics during
training.
```
Ray Tune is a library built into Ray and is designed to simplify and streamline the process
```

of optimizing hyperparameters for ML models. It offers advanced capabilities to explore
the hyperparameter space in an efficient and scalable way, while leveraging the power of
distributed computing. To install this module, run the following command:
```
pip install -U ray[tune]
It also provides advanced logging capabilities by tracking results and supporting tools
```

such as TensorBoard, Weight & Biases, and MLFlow.
```
The optimization process with Ray Tune involves the following steps:

```

• Defining the training function that accepts a dictionary of hyperparameters
• Specifying the space of hyperparameters to explore
• Choosing a search strategy
• Running the tuning process

```
In Chapter 9 , we discussed Deep Learning (DL) while referring to PyTorch as a frame-
```

work to perform ML calculations. Now, in this context, we will integrate Ray to use all the
benefits of distributed (and parallel) computing in Machine Learning. Let us therefore examine the same FashionCNN model used previously and subject it to a series of operations
performed by the advanced modules Ray Train, Ray Tune and Ray Serve.
```
First of all, since it is a neural network model, its efficiency in learning and the accuracy
```

of its predictions will be linked to a series of hyperparameters. We will use the power of
distributed computing to test a whole series of values of these parameters to see which of
them will be the most efficient. To do so, we will use both Ray Train and Ray Tune at the
same time.
```
In many versions, Ray Tune (but not only, also the other modules) often has problems
```

when you are logging it with TensorBoardX. To eliminate the problem, uninstall the module
via:
```
pip uninstall tensorboardX
Now, let us implement the code for tuning hyperparameters during training. We will
```

start with the FashionCNN model and adapt it to this context:
```
# Tuning code
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
```


<a id='p821'></a>
<!-- Página 821 -->

```
821

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
import ray
from ray import tune, train
from ray.tune.schedulers import ASHAScheduler
from ray.tune import CLIReporter
# Definition of the FashionCNN model with Ray Tune
class FashionCNN(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, hidden_units=600):
super(FashionCNN, self).__init__()
self.layer1 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),

nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)
)
self.layer2 = nn.Sequential(
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=32, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3),
nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
nn.ReLU(),
nn.MaxPool2d(2)
)
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=64*6*6, out_features=hidden_units)
self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.25)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=hidden_units, out_features=120)
self.fc3 = nn.Linear(in_features=120, out_features=10)
def forward(self, x):
x = self.layer1(x)
x = self.layer2(x)
x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
x = self.fc1(x)
x = self.dropout(x)
x = self.fc2(x)
x = self.fc3(x)
return x
```

In Chapter 8 , we performed a simple training with a fixed set of hyperparameters chosen from other similar models or taken from literature. Now, we will apply both Ray Train
and Ray Tune to this model and elaborate an estimate of the best hyperparameters, while
activating a form of training in a distributed (and parallel) system to make this operation
highly efficient.

<a id='p822'></a>
<!-- Página 822 -->

822

First, let us take care of training the model and specify a train_fashion_mnist
```
function with the functions made available by Ray Train:
def train_fashion_mnist(config):
# Dataset and transforms
transform = transforms.Compose([
transforms.ToTensor(),
transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))
])
train_dataset = datasets.FashionMNIST(
root=".data",
train=True,
download=True,
transform=transform
)
train_loader = DataLoader(
dataset=train_dataset,
batch_size=int(config["batch_size"]),
shuffle=True
)
# Model initialization
model = FashionCNN(hidden_units=int(config["hidden_units"]))
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=config["lr"])
# Training loop
for epoch in range(5):
model.train()
running_loss = 0.0
for images, labels in train_loader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
outputs = model(images)
loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
running_loss += loss.item()
# Record loss per epoch
train.report({"loss": running_loss / len(train_loader)})
```

This function accepts as a parameter ( config ) the configuration to test sent by
Ray Tune, which contains one of the possible combinations of hyperparameters. These
combinations are chosen based on the values defined by the hyperparameter space that
have to be added to the previous code.
```
# Hyperparameter Space
search_space = {
```


<a id='p823'></a>
<!-- Página 823 -->

```
823

"lr": tune.loguniform(1e-4, 1e-1),
"batch_size": tune.choice([32, 64, 128]),
"hidden_units": tune.choice([400, 600, 800])
}
As we can see, we have given Ray Tune three possible choices (via tune.choice )
```

of configuration of the hidden layer units and the batch size to use in the learning phase.
Furthermore, we have also defined a learning rate range between 0.1 and 0.0001.
```
While analyzing the code of the function inside it, we can see that the images of the
```

FashionMNIST dataset (28x28) are preprocessed using transforms.Compose . This
first converts them into a PyTorch tensor via the transforms.ToTensor() method
and then normalizes the pixel values with a mean of 0.5 and a standard deviation of 0.5 with
transform.Normalize() .
```
DataLoader takes care of loading the dataset, setting the batch size based on the configu-
```

ration to be passed to the function. Furthermore, thanks to shuffle=True, the data is mixed
to avoid recurring patterns.
```
At this point, the FashionCNN model is ready to be initialized with a hidden layer with
```

different units, depending on the configuration to be tested. This parameter is very important because it modifies the neural network itself and its ability to learn. Then the loss and
optimization functions are defined: CrossEntropyLoss suitable for multi-class classification problems and Adam, an optimizer with a learning rate that also varies with the
past configuration. Training occurs in five epochs with a repeated cycle for each batch.

• A forward pass is performed to calculate the predictions.
• The loss is calculated by comparing the predictions with the real labels.
• A backward pass is performed to calculate the gradients.
• The weights of the model are updated with the optimizer.

Finally, at the end of each epoch, the average loss is calculated (on the training dataset)
and recorded via train.report() . This value is sent to Ray Tune which uses it to
establish which are the best hyperparameters.
Another function to define is the one that regulates the tuning, which we will call
tune_fashion_mnist . Here, we will set its configuration through a series of parameters shown as follows:
```
# Ray Tune configuration
def tune_fashion_mnist():
scheduler = ASHAScheduler(
max_t=5,
grace_period=1,
reduction_factor=2
)
reporter = CLIReporter(
metric_columns=["loss", "training_iteration"]
```


<a id='p824'></a>
<!-- Página 824 -->

824

```
)
result = tune.run(
train_fashion_mnist,
resources_per_trial={"cpu": 1, "gpu": 0},
config=search_space,
metric="loss",
mode="min",
num_samples=10,
scheduler=scheduler,
progress_reporter=reporter,
storage_path="/home/myname/ray_results"
)
# Return the best hyperparameters
best_trial = result.get_best_trial("loss", "min", "last")
print(f"Best trial config: {best_trial.config}")
print(f"Best trial final loss: {best_trial.last_result['loss']}")
In the function code, the ASHAScheduler (Asynchronous Successive Halving Algorithm)
```

is defined, which is used to manage the tuning process through a series of parameters
such as max_t=5, which defines the maximum number of epochs for training;
grace_period=1 in which at least 1 epoch is guaranteed before interrupting the test;
and reduction_factor=2 in which the least promising tests are eliminated. This
halves the number of tests at each stage. The purpose of this scheduler is therefore to
reduce computational costs by performing and filtering the most promising tests.
```
Another object defined within the function is the CLIReporter which is used to
```

monitor the progress of the tuning in the terminal through the metric_columns parameter. This parameter displays the variables on the terminal during tuning, which in
our case is loss and training_iteration .
```
Finally, the tuning is started via tune.run , where the Ray Train training function
```

( train_fashion_mnist ) is along with the resources available for each trial, the
search space of the hyperparameters to be considered, the metrics to be minimized, the total
number of combinations to be considered ( num_samples=10 ), and the scheduler to
be used. The results will finally be displayed in output on the console.
```
You can start the tuning directly via the following lines of code:
# Starting Ray Tune
if __name__ == "__main__":
ray.init(_temp_dir="/home/myname/ray_temp")
tune_fashion_mnist()
ray.shutdown()

Modin as a Parallel Alternative to
Pandas

Modin is an open-source library designed to streamline and parallelize data analysis operations in Python and is a high-performance alternative to Pandas. Maintaining the
same API as Pandas, Modin allows you to scale operations on large datasets by leveraging
multiple cores and distributed resources such as CPU clusters, GPUs, and clouds. Thanks
to its compatibility with Pandas syntax, Modin allows users to improve performance without changing the existing code, which makes this transition particularly easy for those who
already use Pandas.
Data analysis libraries such as Pandas are essential for data manipulation in Python.
However, Pandas is primarily optimized for single-core computation, which can be limiting
for large datasets. Modin addresses this limitation by introducing multi-core parallelism
and support for distributed infrastructure such as CPU and GPU clusters by using backends
such as Ray and Dask to distribute tasks across multiple resources. Also, Modin is uniquely
designed to manipulate tabular data in a scalable manner. It takes advantage of parallelism
in distributed environments. The transition from Pandas to Modin is almost natural and
can be done very easily.
Modin installation is simple and can be done with the following pip. Since this library
also requires you to install distributed computing engine, you can choose which backend to
use (Ray or Dask) at the time of installation.
```
pip install modin[ray]
```

or
```
pip install modin[dask]
```

If you install Modin without specifying a backend, recent versions will default to Ray as
the execution engine.
After installing it, you can start using it by importing Modin instead of Pandas.
```
import modin.pandas as pd # Replacing Pandas with Modin
```

Once configured, Modin automatically distributes operations across multiple cores, while
accelerating processing without the need to modify the original code. Let us look at a very
simple example where we load a CSV file via Pandas.
```
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("employees.csv")

833
```

We can now bring all these operations to work in a distributed system simply by replacing Pandas with Modin in the import line via:
```
import modin.pandas as pd

As we have seen, the code and syntax remain the same and only the module import is
changed. The results are identical, but in the second case, the active distribution service
begins, which in this example is the Ray instance. For such a small and simple CSV file,
enabling distribution does not provide any meaningful benefit. However, this approach
becomes useful when dealing with large CSV files.

Although the CSV file in this example is nearly 3 GB in size, the performance difference is
```

not particularly pronounced. This is mainly because the benchmark was executed locally:
although the machine had 12 CPUs available, only 8 were allocated to Ray to avoid saturating system resources. Pandas, being optimized for single-node execution, was able to
exploit local performance efficiently. In a cluster environment where Pandas cannot operate, the number of workers available to Ray would have been higher, which would reduce
execution times. Furthermore, the packages must be distributed. This would requires
time and resources that would have to be subtracted from the general performance. Here,
Pandas does not have to compensate locally, and thus gains efficiency. By increasing the
size of the CSV file, loading it into memory as a DataFrame will be impossible locally due to
memory issues. Therefore, the choice to operate in a distributed manner will be a preferential and not the default. In the previous example, we used aggregation operations (such
as mean ) and grouping operations using GroupBy on the DataFrame, where
distributed calculations offered by Modin are more efficient. Another type of operation
on DataFrames that can be optimized with Modin is Join and Merge. This time we will create an example where we will generate two large datasets on which we will then perform
these operations under benchmark. We will measure the difference in performance here
as well.

import numpy as np
import ray

```
import modin.config as cfg
def generate_large_datasets(rows=10**6):
np.random.seed(42)
data1 = {
"key": np.random.randint(1, rows // 10, size=rows),
"value1": np.random.rand(rows),
}
df1 = pd.DataFrame(data1)
data2 = {
"key": np.random.randint(1, rows // 10, size=rows),
"value2": np.random.rand(rows),
}
df2 = pd.DataFrame(data2)
return df1, df2
def benchmark_pandas_merge(df1, df2):
print("\n------- Pandas -----------")
start = time.time()
df_pandas1 = df1.copy()
df_pandas2 = df2.copy()
merged_pandas = df_pandas1.merge(df_pandas2, on="key", how="inner")
pandas_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Elapsed time with Pandas for Merge: {pandas_time:.2f} sec.")

print(merged_pandas.head())
def benchmark_modin_merge(df1, df2):
print("\n------- Modin -----------")
start = time.time()
df_modin1 = df1.copy()
df_modin2 = df2.copy()
merged_modin = df_modin1.merge(df_modin2, on="key", how="inner")
modin_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Elapsed time with Modin for Merge: {modin_time:.2f} sec.")
print(merged_modin.head())
```

Once the code is inserted, we will create the two datasets and measure the performances.

```
df1, df2 = generate_large_datasets(rows=10**7)
benchmark_pandas_merge(df1, df2)
benchmark_modin_merge(df1, df2)
```

In this case, two datasets with 10 million rows were generated, since creating larger
datasets was not feasible on a local system due to limited memory resources.

Modin as a Ray-Integrated Tool

We have seen that Modin uses Ray as a backend to distribute the computation on tabular
datasets. Now, let us reverse the main concerns of this chapter. We started by talking
about the Ray framework and its specific use in ML with Ray Tune and Ray Serve that extend it to distributed systems. We will also consider Modin as a tool to integrate into the
Ray ecosystem and will use it to manage larger tabular datasets or simulate parallel preprocessing operations before passing the data to the model. An example for explanatory
purposes can be the following one. Here, the dataset that is to be subjected to the ML
model is present in a large CSV file of that a single machine will not able to manage.
```
import modin.pandas as pd
def preprocess_data(file_path):
print("Loading dataset with Modin..")
# Parallel loading
data = pd.read_csv(file_path)
data["label_normalized"] = data["label"] / data["label"].max()
print("Pre-processing completed!")
return data
metadata = preprocess_data("fashion_metadata.csv")
```

The content of the CSV file is loaded in a distributed manner in a cluster of machines,
where each of them is assigned a portion of the content to work on. Even the preprocessing (here represented by a simple normalization) is carried out in parallel between
the various machines present in the cluster.

Comparison of Ray, Dask, and Celery:
Architecture and Performance

We have now arrived at the end of this chapter. Let us look at the entire distributed
computing environment through the following frameworks and compare them:

• Ray
• Dask
• Celery

All three of them are designed to solve parallelization and resource distribution problems. They also share the goal of distributing tasks across multiple cores or nodes. So,
which one should you choose?
First, these three frameworks have different architectures and performance. Furthermore, despite their common goals, each framework is optimized for specific types of
workloads like managing asynchronous tasks and scaling machine learning applications.
Therefore, you should choose which framework to use based on the specific area in which
you want to use distributed computing.

• Ray : Distributed Computing and ML
• Dask : DAG and Cluster for Big Data and Data Science
• Celery : Asynchronous Task Queues for Job Background

```
As we have seen in this chapter, Ray is particularly suited for distributed machine learn-
```

ing, reinforcement learning, and hyperparameter tuning applications. Advanced modules
such as Ray Tune and Ray Serve are ideal for large-scale distributed AI pipelines. Dask
is designed for distributed computing on CPU and GPU clusters as it has a Directed Acyclic
Graph (DAG)-based architecture.
```
This approach makes Dask ideal for tasks with many dependencies, such as data analysis
```

pipelines and Big Data processing. Dask is also compatible with Pandas and NumPy, which
makes it easy to migrate data science operations to a larger scale.
```
Celery is an asynchronous task framework that uses message queues like Redis or Rab-
```

bitMQ to handle the execution of background tasks. It is particularly useful for repetitive
or non-real-time critical tasks such as sending emails, file processing, and ETL pipelines.

```

Introduction

PySpark is the Python API which works with Apache Spark, an open-source framework
for distributed computing and processing of large volumes of data. PySpark allows you
to harness the power of Spark using a more accessible language such as Python, without
having to necessarily write code in Java or Scala.
In this chapter, we will introduce the core concepts of PySpark and illustrate its execution model for distributed data processing. You will learn how to create and manipulate
distributed datasets, apply transformations and actions, and understand how Spark executes operations across a cluster. By the end of the chapter, you will be able to identify
appropriate use cases for PySpark, and build simple, scalable data processing pipelines.

## 854 STRUCTURE


<a id='p855'></a>
<!-- Página 855 -->

Apache Spark

Apache Spark is one of the most popular and powerful platforms for distributed processing of large volumes of data. Designed to be fast, flexible and easy to use, Spark has
revolutionized the way data is managed and analyzed at scale. Born as an open-source
project at UC Berkeley in 2009, Spark has quickly become a reference tool in the Big Data
ecosystem.
```
From a more technical point of view, Apache Spark is a distributed computing frame-
```

work that allows you to process data on clusters of computers in a scalable and resilient
way. Unlike other distributed computing frameworks, Spark stands out for its speed,
flexibility and ease of use.
```
Thanks to the in-memory computation engine, Spark is able to process data much faster
```

than other systems. It also supports a wide range of workloads like batch processing,
real-time analytics, Machine Learning (ML) and graph processing, which make it one of the
most flexible distributed systems in its field of use. It is also very simple due to its intuitive
API and is available in different languages such as Python, Java, Scala and R.
```
Spark offers an integrated ecosystem of the following modules that allow you to tackle
```

different types of processing:

• SparkSQL for working with structured data using SQL and DataFrames
• Spark Streaming to process data streams in real-time
• MLlib, a scalable ML library
• GraphX to process and analyze graphs (not supported in Python)
• Spark Core, the main engine for managing distributed computing and resources

Furthermore, Spark can operate in many cluster platforms that range from a simple
standalone cluster to Apache Hadoop and Apache Mesos systems, and containerized systems
such as Kubernetes.
Thanks to all these features, Apache Spark has become an essential tool for those who
want to extract value from data.




```
855
```


<a id='p856'></a>
<!-- Página 856 -->


## 856 APACHE SPARK


<a id='p857'></a>
<!-- Página 857 -->

PySpark

PySpark is the Apache Spark API designed to enable Python developers to harness the
power of Spark’s distributed computing. Due to its ease of use and the flexibility of Python,
PySpark represents an ideal bridge between the world of Big data and the community of
developers, data scientists, and analysts who work with Python on a daily basis.
You can install PySpark directly via this pip:
```
pip install pyspark
```

PySpark is structured to provide Python developers with an interface to interact with
Apache Spark functionality. Its structure is composed of several core modules, each designed for a specific task.
```
SparkContext is the heart of every Spark application. It takes connects to the Spark
```

cluster and coordinates the distribution of operations among the cluster nodes. When
a working session ( SparkSession ) is created, PySpark automatically starts a
SparkContext instance. The Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD) is the basic
element for Spark and represents a distributed collection of immutable objects that can be
processed in parallel. Once created, these objects cannot be modified and in case of error,
RDDs are regenerated by Spark. Two different types of operations are performed on these
objects, which are:

• Transformations (Lazy)
• Actions (Eager)

```
Transformations are ” lazy ” operations (executed only when requested) such as
```

map , filter , and groupBy . On the other hand, actions are ” eager
” operations (executed when declared) that produce a result and start data processing such
as collect , count , and take . DataFrames are an evolved form of
RDDs, and are very similar to those used in Pandas, but are optimized to be instantiated and
processed in a distributed manner. On these structured or semi-structured octets, PySpark
offers a large set of intuitive methods for manipulating the data contained within them.
Furthermore, by exploiting the Catalyst engine, PySpark allows you to use SQL-like query
methods to apply to DataFrames. In fact, SparkSQL is a module that can be integrated
into the framework that allows you to work on data using SQL syntax: DataFrames are
recorded as temporary tables on which to execute SQL queries. Another very important
tool in the Spark ecosystem is the Machine Learning Library (MLlib), which can also be

```
857
```


<a id='p858'></a>
<!-- Página 858 -->

858 PYSPARK

used with PySpark . It is a real library that provides a large set of algorithms for regression, classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction and model evaluation. Spark is a
suitable tool for processing Big Data. However, there are others for streaming data. For
instance, Spark Streaming, which is based on micro batches, allows processing data streams
in real-time. Structured Streaming is a more recent approach to streaming and is based
on the use of DataFrame for real-time data analysis. Finally, GraphFrame is a support
tool for graph processing for Python (as GraphX is for Scala) of the Spark ecosystem.
```
Once you install PySpark on your system, you can create a session called SparkSession
```

, which will be the main access point for all Spark resources, contexts and modules.
PySpark can run both in local mode (standalone) and connected to a remote Spark cluster
(distributed mode). In local mode, PySpark uses your computer as a Spark environment
and emulates the behavior of a cluster without connecting to an external Spark server.
This mode is useful in the development or testing phase and allows you to work on small
datasets. This configuration is simple to use since it does not require any additional installation. It is set automatically or explicitly specified in the SparkSession through the
master("local[*]") method. In particular, the asterisk inside the square brackets
indicates that the SparkSession will have to use all available resources (all CPUs).
```
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder \
.appName("PySpark in local mode") \
.master("local[*]") \
.getOrCreate()
However, the configuration you should work with is connected to a remote Spark server.
```

It allows you to take advantage of the benefits of parallel computing and distributed processing across multiple available resources. To do this, Spark uses one of the following
cluster managers:

• YARN (on Hadoop systems)
• Mesos (on generic clusters)
• Kubernetes (on containerized clusters)

```
In this case, we will specify in the master method the IP address of the server with the
```

port related to the service.
```
spark = SparkSession.builder \
.appName("PySpark in cluster mode") \
.master("spark://10.0.0.27:7077") \ # example of URL address
.getOrCreate()
To check the active configuration in the code you can use:
print(spark.sparkContext.master)
This will return the operating mode: local[*] or the URL of the Spark server.
Once all the calculations are completed, you will have to close the session and we can do
```

this by adding the following at the end of the code:

<a id='p859'></a>
<!-- Página 859 -->

```
859

spark.stop()
This ensures proper cleanup of resources at the end of a Spark application or script.
Also, it may be necessary to configure some environment variables in the system de-
```

pending on the features used, the operating system, and the applications installed. On
Ubuntu, for example, you only need a Java JDK installed for Spark to run. PySpark itself
must be installed separately via:
```
pip install pyspark,
This can be done unless you are running Spark from the official distribution, where PyS-
```

park is already bundled.
```
The only necessary step is to install Java JDK on Ubuntu, which is necessary to run the
```

Spark ecosystem that runs on Java. This looks like the following:

After the installation is complete, set the global variable JAVA_HOME in the
```

Before starting, it would be good to dedicate a virtual environment to work with PySpark
```

through:

Note : With PySpark, it is preferable to work with Linux systems to minimize the possi-

bility of problems related to incompatibility and dependencies between the different versions
present. It is also easier to manage any visibility between them.

These are very common operations that are applied to Spark DataFrame and have the
```

same syntax as a Pandas DataFrame. However, it is possible to perform similar operations
using a completely different approach. For those who are used to working and manipulating data in database tables, they will be more comfortable using SQL queries. We have
already established that it is possible to use SQL-like queries on Spark DataFrame thanks to
SparkSQL. Let us see how to apply SQL queries to the previous DataFrame.

The first step will be to register the DataFrame as a temporary table to execute SQL

queries, regardless of the type of search or selection that we want to apply to the data.

Now, we will perform operations like the previous transformations filter, groupBy
and orderBy ), but using an SQL-like language. To do this, there is a specific function
spark.sql(, in which the SQL query is passed as a string argument. For example, if

A More Complex Example
Introducing a Parallel Calculation

The previous example was simple, but a great explainer of the features offered by PySpark
to operate and manipulate a DataFrame and the data contained within it. Now let us
move on to another example which is slightly more complex and highlights the advantages
of parallel computing offered by the distributed environments on which PySpark works.
Here, we use the concept of Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD) to perform a parallel
mapping and reduction operation, while simulating a distributed analysis.
```
Imagine that we have a large text dataset, and we want to calculate the frequency of
```

words in a parallel way. Let us reopen a new Spark session locally, and define a list of
strings as follows:

PySpark supports parallel computing",
with Spark we can process large volumes of data",]

The input is transformed into an RDD distributed across the available cores. PySpark
```

divides the work into multiple partitions to process the data in parallel. Now, let us perform
a parallel word count through the following code:

word_pairs = words.map(lambda word: (word.lower(), 1))
word_counts = word_pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
df_word_counts = word_counts.toDF(["Word", "Count"]).orderBy("Count",
```

ascending=False)

are explained as follows:

• map associate each word with the value 1.

the counts.

Since PySpark operates in lazy mode, the reduceByKey operation is optimized to reduce

the data locally on each node before combining the results. Finally, the final results are

Distributed Computing Optimization

Distributed computing optimization is essential to make the most of a cluster’s resources
and improve the performance of PySpark applications. There are several key aspects that
can be useful in this regard. A simple but effective example to explain and get familiar
with these aspects could be to choose a dataset containing a series of data such as financial
transactions, and then process it.
```
Let us start by setting up a simple-to-use dataset, which we will call transactions.csv
```

:
```
user_id,amount
1,100
2,200
1,300
2,400
3,500
First, let us implement some basic code to read the file, process the data, and calculate
```

the total sum and average transactions per user. Write the following code to a file and save
it, for example, as optimized.py :
```
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder \
.appName("Distributed Optimization") \
.master("local[*]") \
.getOrCreate()
# Read CSV file as RDD
rdd = spark.sparkContext.textFile("file:///transactions.csv")
# Transform data into (user_id, amount)
header = rdd.first() # Salta l'header
data = rdd.filter(lambda row: row != header) \
.map(lambda row: row.split(",")) \
.map(lambda cols: (int(cols[0]), float(cols[1])))
# Calculate the sum and average of transactions per user
user_totals = data.mapValues(lambda amount: (amount, 1)) \
.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1])) \
.mapValues(lambda x: (x[0], x[0] / x[1]))
print(user_totals.collect())

873
```


<a id='p874'></a>
<!-- Página 874 -->

874 DISTRIBUTED COMPUTING OPTIMIZATION

```
spark.stop()
Running it will get us the following results:
[(2, (600.0, 300.0)), (1, ((400.0, 200.0)), (3, (500.0, 500.0))]
Although we have used a very small dataset for convenience, it is sufficient to explain
```

the optimization aspects. The first optimization we will talk about is efficient partitioning . Partitioning is how Spark divides data into smaller chunks, called partitions, that
are distributed and processed across the cluster nodes. Each partition is processed by a
single task. This is important because it introduces parallelism, which means that more
partitions/nodes can work at the same time. Spark does this automatically, but there are
situations where this may not be optimal. In fact, while automatic partitioning works in
most cases, there are situations where manual partitioning is useful. This is possible
in Spark using the repartition() method, which takes as a parameter the number
of partitions to use. In fact, the automatic process could use too many partitions for the
necessary calculations, which can create an overhead and make the calculation inefficient.
In a large cluster, automatic partitioning might not be able to make the most of all the
available resources.
```
Starting from the previous code, we will divide the data into 4 partitions, while inserting
```

the following line immediately after defining the data :
```
data = data.repartition(4)
Another approach to optimization is persistence and caching . If the data will be
```

reused in multiple operations, we can store it in memory to avoid recalculations. For this
purpose, we will use the cache() function. Replace the previously updated line
with this command:
```
data.cache()
This instruction activates caching, which means that the data will be stored in memory
```

for quick access. This operation reduces the processing time for repeated passes. In
addition, with persist( ) it is possible to choose the specific level of storage of data,
as shown here:
```
data.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
Another optimization approach that can be applied to the example code is filtering via
```

broadcast variables . These allow you to share small datasets or reference values among
all the nodes in a cluster without replicating them. Without broadcast, Spark ships a copy
of the variable with every task, which leads to significant network overhead . Suppose
we have a list of VIP users that we want to use as a reference to filter the data:
```
# VIP User List
vip_users = [1, 2]
# Filter VIP users only
vip_data = data.filter(lambda x: x[0] in vip_users)
With this code, we will have a separate copy of vip_users for each task. When
```

you use this list in the code without broadcast variables, each task gets a separate copy of
the vip_users list. This means that if you have 1,000 tasks, the list will be replicated 1,000
times. Each node will get a separate copy of the list from the driver creating network

<a id='p875'></a>
<!-- Página 875 -->

```
875

```

overhead. Also, there will be a waste of memory, since each task stores a separate copy
that consumes memory.
```
Let us introduce a broadcast variable in the code by passing the list of VIP users as an
```

argument to broadcast() :
```
# VIP User List
vip_users = [1, 2]
# List broadcast
broadcast_vip = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(vip_users)
# Filter VIP users only
vip_data = data.filter(lambda x: x[0] in broadcast_vip.value)
In this case, the driver will send a single copy of the vip_user list to each node.
```

Each node stores this copy in memory and shares it with all tasks running on that node.
Tasks access the broadcast list as a global reference without creating separate copies. This
way, the VIP user list is shared efficiently across all nodes, while reducing network traffic
and ensuring quick processing.
```
Another optimization is to carefully choose between reduceByKey and combineByKey
```

. Both operations can trigger shuffles when data needs to be grouped by key, which is
costly in terms of time and resources due to data transfers and (de)serialization overhead.
```
The key difference is that reduceByKey applies the same function both within and across
```

partitions, while combineByKey allows you to define separate functions for creating while
merging within and across partitions. This makes combineByKey more flexible, though
not necessarily efficient in every case. Minimizing unnecessary shuffles in either case
significantly improves performance. For our example, we can replace user_totals
in the code with the following definition:
```
user_totals_optimized = data.combineByKey(
lambda value: (value, 1), # Initialization
lambda acc, value: (acc[0] + value, acc[1] + 1), # within the partition

lambda acc1, acc2: (acc1[0] + acc2[0], acc1[1] + acc2[1]) # between
```

partitions
```
).mapValues(lambda x: (x[0], x[0] / x[1]))
The combineByKey function combines data locally before transferring it between
```

partitions. This reduces the number of shuffles, while improving performance.
```
Another optimization is the switch to DataFrame. This operation will allow us to take
```

advantage of more efficient components within PySpark such as Catalyst Optimizer and
Tungsten Execution Engine . Catalyst Optimizer is the optimization engine for queries
on DataFrame and SQL in Spark. This component performs logical and physical transformations to improve execution. Tungsten Execution Engine optimizes the use of CPU and
memory through binary data formats and low-level operations. Therefore, switching data
to Spark DataFrame automatically improves queries on that data and makes them faster.
It also reduces the number of operations needed and optimizes the use of resources.
Furthermore, it can also be said that the code becomes simpler and more readable. To do

follows:

Using toDF() to convert an RDD to a Spark Dataframe increases performance, but
```

in cases where it is possible, like our example, further performance optimization is required
to read the data source directly as a DataFrame. In our case, since it is a CSV file, a
particular construct is used:
```
df = spark.read.format("csv") \
```


<a id='p877'></a>
<!-- Página 877 -->

```
877

.option("header", "true") \ # Indicates that the file has a header
.option("inferSchema", "true") \ # Automatically infers data types
.load("transactions.csv")
When reading a file directly as a DataFrame, Spark takes full advantage of the Cata-
```

lyst Optimizer which uses techniques such as column pruning (reading only the necessary
columns) and filter pushdown (by applying filters as soon as possible to avoid loading unnecessary data). Additionally, an RDD stores data as Python objects, which are less memory
efficient. A DataFrame, on the other hand, uses an optimized binary format (Tungsten
Execution Engine) which allows for more efficient memory and CPU management. Spark
offers optimized native readers for many file formats such as CSV, Parquet, and JSON.
```
The initial code of optimized.py then becomes very simple and readable. It
```

looks something like this:

.master("local[*]") \
.getOrCreate()
df = spark.read.format("csv") \
.option("header", "true") \ # Indicates that the file has a header
.option("inferSchema", "true") \ # Automatically infers data types
.load("file:///path/to/transactions.csv")
df.printSchema()
df.show()

Spark UI

While running a Spark Session, you can visit the Spark UI by opening a browser and connecting to http://localhost:4040. You will see a screen like the one in Figure 12.1 :
```
Figure 12.1: Spark Web Tools Accessed via Port 4040
```

This web interface provides a detailed view of Spark applications with useful information for many operations such as:

• Monitoring job progress
• Performance analysis
• Identifying bottlenecks
• Diagnosing errors and various problems

The interface is divided into several sections, each of which provides detailed information as follows:

• Jobs shows a list of all jobs executed or running with related information (status,
```
number of tasks, execution time).
```

• Stages shows the details of the stages in each job. A stage is a set of parallel tasks
```
that follow the same type of operation (for example, map or reduce). The related
information (number of tasks, execution time, operations performed, shuffle details)
is shown here as well.
```

• Tasks displays detailed information about individual tasks executed within a stage,
```
along with related information (status, execution time, CPU and memory usage, amount
of data read and written).
```

• Storage displays information about datasets stored in memory or on disk, which
```
includes both RDD and DataFrame.
```

• Environment shows Spark environment information (component and dependency
```
versions, environment variables, and configurations).
```

• Executors shows information about running executors. These are the processes
```
that run tasks distributed across the cluster nodes.

```

Spark UI can become an essential tool for monitoring and optimizing Spark applications.

Spark Streaming and Real-Time Data
Processing

At the beginning of the chapter we talked about PySpark allowing real-time data processing
with two different approaches:

• Spark Streaming
• Structured Streaming

```
Spark Streaming is an Apache Spark module designed for real-time data stream pro-
```

cessing and is based on the concept of micro-batches. It collects data in small time windows (batches) and processes them sequentially. Each time interval produces a new RDD,
which represents the data in the micro-batch. At the end, you get a continuous sequence
of RDDs. This concept is called Dstream (Discretized Stream) .
```
Structured Streaming is based on the DataFrame extension for structured stream
```

processing.
```
However, the most modern and recommended approach for processing streaming data
```

with PySpark is Structured Streaming. In fact, Dstream has been “deprecated” since
version 3.4, and it is therefore advisable to abandon this approach in favor of Structured
Streaming, which is based on the use of DataFrames.
```

socket (for example a local server) and calculates the word rate in real-time:

# Reading data stream from a socket
lines = spark.readStream \
.format("socket") \
.option("host", "localhost") \

This command launches the TCP server with two options: (-l) which indicates that the
```

server must work in “listener” mode, that is, it must remain listening for incoming connections; the option (-k) makes NetCat accept multiple consecutive connections. Without this
option, the listener would close after accepting a single connection. As for the port, the

Collecting Results on Storage Systems

In the previous case, we saw all that all the results were reported on the console. This is a
very simple case, which is apt for educational or debugging purposes. In the real world,
the results obtained from the streaming computation will have to be stored on some form of
storage or an additional processing and analysis platform (HDFS files, S3, Kafka or an SQL
database). In the example code for writing to the console, we have used ” complete
” as the output mode, but Spark Streaming offers three different output modes, which are:

• Complete writes all the resulting data to each batch (the one we used in the
```
output).
```

• Append writes only the new lines added in the current batch.
• Update writes only updated rows from the previous batch (not always supported).

Instead of displaying our results on the console, we will write them to a Parquet file,
which is a columnar format and is highly efficient and compatible with Spark (and many
other systems), without the need for extra manipulation.
However, since it is written to a file, we need to make some changes to the previous code.
First, we set the output mode to “append”. We also need to add a watermark. This is
a mechanism that allows Spark to handle late data and determine when older data can be
removed from the state inside the aggregation. So, the watermark specifies a time limit
for the data that can be considered for aggregation. This requires that the data has a
timestamp.
When finished, the code will look like the following example. Write it to a text file and
save it as stream2.py .

# Word count with watermark and windowing
word_counts = words \
.withWatermark("timestamp", "10 seconds") \
.groupBy(
window("timestamp", "1 minute"),
"word"
).count()
# Writing results in Parquet format
query = word_counts.writeStream \
.outputMode("append") \ # Please, read the note below the code!
.format("parquet") \
.option("path", "output") \
.option("checkpointLocation", "checkpoint") \
.start()
# Waiting and terminating the job
query.awaitTermination(300)
print("Stop of acquisition time")
# Spark session closure
spark.stop()
print("Spark Session closed. Check results in output directory.")
Note : Using outputMode(“append”) with aggregations requires event-time processing
```

with a watermark. Without a watermark, Spark cannot determine when a window is complete and will raise an error. In the example above, we will parse the event timestamp from
the incoming data and set a 10-second watermark, which tells Spark when it is safe to finalize
windows and emit results incrementally.
```
The Parquet format is suitable for this operation as it supports complex structures and
```

is optimized for analytical queries with Spark and other tools. This format is compatible
with many frameworks like Pandas and Hadoop.

<a id='p887'></a>
<!-- Página 887 -->

```
887

As part of the code changes, we have set the watermark to ignore data with timestamps
```

delayed by more than 10 seconds compared to it. The 1-minute time window groups the
data by time intervals.
```
A timestamp column is also added to the two existing columns (words and count). As
```

in the previous case, the text is divided into words using split and explode creating a new
row in the DataFrame for each of these words.
```
The results are written in Parquet format in the output directory, together with a check-
```

should be empty. To facilitate this task at each execution, it will be simple to launch the
following commands in sequence:
```

$ mkdir output checkpoint
The start() method starts the streaming query while awaitTermination()
```

takes the time the application runs for as a parameter. The stop() command finally
closes the Spark session and frees up resources. Text strings warn in console output when
streaming is started and when it is closed.
```
The ” append ” mode (the only one applicable to writing parquet files) writes the
```

new batches of data without overwriting those already saved.
```

Kafka

Kafka is an open-source platform for real-time messaging and data stream processing.
It works as a pub-sub (publish/subscribe) messaging system and allows producers and
consumers to communicate asynchronously.
```
Kafka is composed of:

```

• Broker servers that handle message traffic
• Producer that posts messages on a topic
• Consumer that reads messages from a topic
• Topic , which is a logical channel to organize messages and is divided into partitions
```
to improve scalability

Writing Data to HDFS or Amazon S3

Spark is an extremely flexible system; therefore, it is possible to switch the saving of extracted data from local to external storage easily, while making small changes to the codes
created.
Among the most commonly used destinations in this type of distributed system such are
HDFS and S3.
```
Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is a distributed file system designed to man-
```

age large amounts of data on computer clusters. It is a fundamental part of the Hadoop
ecosystem and allows you to store data in a distributed manner on multiple nodes. The
files are divided into blocks (generally 128MB or 256MB) and then distributed on different
nodes of the cluster. Each of these blocks is replicated on multiple nodes, ensuring that
the data is available even in the event of a node failure.
```
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is a scalable cloud storage service offered by
```

Amazon Web Services (AWS) and is designed to store and retrieve virtually unlimited amounts
of data. Being a cloud service, data is accessible everywhere via the internet.
The choice between these two will depend on the needs of your project, the available
infrastructure and the desired architecture.
HDFS is ideal for local environments (on-premises) and is useful for traditional ETL processes and long-term archiving on Hadoop clusters.
```
S3 instead is perfect for cloud scenarios, when data will need to be accessible globally or
```

to AWS systems (Redshift, Athena, SageMaker).
Considering the previous example with Kafka, in order to write the result of our processing, it is sufficient to change the output and the checkpoint path within the kafka.py
code.
If you want to save your data to an HDFS cluster, you can simply change the output path.
Spark supports HDFS natively and can therefore specify an HDFS path as the destination.
This is shown in the following code:
```

.outputMode("append") \
.format("parquet") \
.option("checkpointLocation", "hdfs://<HDFS-NAME-NODE>:9000/checkpoint")
```

GraphFrame

GraphFrame is an Apache Spark-based library designed for graph processing and analysis. Unlike GraphX, which is only developed in Scala and Java, GraphFrame is natively
available for PySpark, which makes it the ideal choice for those who work with Python and
need to manage distributed graphs. Due to its integration with Spark SQL and DataFrame,
GraphFrame provides a simple and powerful interface to represent, manipulate, and analyze graphs, while combining the processing capabilities of Spark with advanced graph
analysis algorithms.
GraphFrame extends the GraphX data model, while relying on DataFrame to represent
edges and nodes. The model is called GraphFrame and is made up of two DataFrames:

```
• Vertices , that represent the nodes of the graph, where each node identified by a
unique ID and additional properties
• Edges, that represent the connections between nodes, with each edge identified by
a source ID ( srv ), a destination ID ( dst ), and optional properties

```

Let us now implement an example to understand how to create a graph. This is an example shows a very simplified social network where people are associated with each other
through a set of relationships that form a graph.
First of all, you will need to install the library in your virtual environment via:
```
pip install graphframes
```

You also need to download the GraphFrame JAR package. At the moment, the latest
one can be downloaded via:
```
wget https://repos.spark-packages.org/graphframes/graphframes/0.8.4-spark3.5-s_

Otherwise, you can consult the different packages available at https://spark-packages.org/package/gr
```

.
Once the library is installed and the JAR file is downloaded, we will import the necessary
modules and create a SparkSession as follows:
```
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from graphframes import GraphFrame
spark = SparkSession.builder \
.appName("GraphFrame Example") \
.master("local[*]") \

Conclusion

In this chapter, we have addressed all the components offered by PySpark , which is the
perfect combination of the power of the Apache Spark framework and the simplicity of the
Python language. PySpark is therefore a tool for distributed computing and is suitable for
tackling the challenges of Big Data. In the first section, you understood the basic elements
such as the Spark Session , the DataFrame RDDs and its characteristics. Then you had
the opportunity to approach the world of distributed ML via MLlib library, which offers
many models and techniques like other similar libraries such as scikit-learn. We discussed
some performance optimization techniques through simple code examples. Finally, we
delved into the study and analysis of data flows generated in real-time, thanks to Spark
Streaming . We did so while gradually integrating other technologies related to the
Spark ecosystem such as Kafka and the storage of processed data. We closed the chapter
with GraphFrame , which is the Python equivalent of Java’s GraphX and Scala for the
computation and analysis of graphs in a distributed manner.

Introduction

With this chapter, we will conclude our exploration of high-performance and parallel programming tools in Python, while introducing Joblib . This library, although not as
versatile as the tools already seen in the book like Dask, Ray or Spark, excels in targeted
areas and rightfully deserves a place in this book. In fact, Joblib was designed to optimize
specific operations in intensive computing contexts and to improve the scalability of computation pipelines and therefore finds its scope of work in simple parallelization, resulting
in caching and efficiency in serialization. Joblib is therefore proposed as a minimalist
solution for scenarios that do not require the full infrastructure of a distributed system.
It can be seen as a “ lightweight ” tool to improve efficiency and productivity in projects
that do not need the complexity of advanced task management.

Joblib and Its Uses

Joblib is an open-source library written in Python and is designed to make heavy computing more efficient. It focuses on three main areas, which are:

• Process Parallelization
• Data Persistence
• Cache Management

```
Parallelization allows you to run independent operations in parallel, while leveraging
```

the multicore capabilities of modern CPUs. It is particularly useful for accelerating intensive computations without having to write complex processes or thread management code.
For persistence, Joblib offers tools to quickly and efficiently save and load complex Python
objects such as NumPy arrays or machine learning models, thus avoiding the recomputation of expensive results or the retraining of existing models. Finally, cache management
allows you to store the results of computationally heavy functions, further allowing them
to be reused in future executions and optimizing repetitive pipelines and applications.
```
Joblib is a natural choice for improving computational efficiency in Python, thanks to
```

its simplicity and optimized performance. While alternatives like multiprocessing,
concurrent.futures , and pickle exist for parallelization and serialization respectively,
Joblib stands out due to some key features. Its intuitive syntax makes it easy to adopt even
for developers with little experience in parallel computing. Furthermore, it is highly optimized to handle large objects such as NumPy arrays or scikit-learn models, which also
support data compression to improve I/O efficiency. Another distinctive aspect is the
advanced parallelization management, with support for backends such as loky (default),
threading and multiprocessing, each suited to specific types of workloads. Finally, Joblib
is tightly integrated with scikit-learn, which makes it an indispensable tool for both serialization and parallelization of complex operations.

## 918 JOBLIB AND ITS USES

Process Parallelization

Parallelization is a key technique for accelerating intensive computational operations by
distributing work across multiple CPU cores. Joblib is particularly appreciated for its
ability to handle parallel tasks with a simple and readable syntax, while still offering high
efficiency in contexts where it excels. Unlike more complex libraries such as multiprocessing, Joblib automatically manages the creation and management of processes without
requiring detailed configuration. It also offers high optimization for numerical calculations. Joblib is particularly suited to working with numpy and pandas data structures as
it leverages optimized serialization and efficient memory use.
```
Unlike more heavyweight tools such as Dask or Ray which shine in clustered distributed
```

computing contexts, Joblib is designed for single-machine parallel operations, while maintaining an optimal balance between simplicity and performance.
```
Thanks to constructs such as Parallel and delayed , it is easy to transform an
```

iterative loop into a parallel operation, which makes coding simple and intuitive. Parallel
is the main object that coordinates the parallel execution of tasks. When called, it creates
a pool of separate processes (or threads, depending on your configuration) to perform the
work in parallel. The tasks will be then distributed among the processes, which will work
on a portion of the total load. When finished, Parallel collects the results from all the
processes and returns them as a sorted list, while corresponding to the original order of the
tasks.
```
The delayed() function is used to “ delay ” the execution of an operation.
```

In other words, instead of immediately executing a function, delayed() creates an
object representing the task that will then be passed to Parallel() for execution.
```
The combined use of Parallel() and delayed() makes parallelization
```

extremely simple, avoiding having to manually manage the creation of processes or threads.
Let us see in detail how they work, starting from a simple example and then applying it to
more complex scenarios.
```
Before starting to work, however, it is necessary to check whether joblib is already present
```

on your system. If not, you can simply install it with the following command:
```
pip install joblib
Let us start with the parallelization of a simple calculation like the square of a number,
```

while using multiple cores in parallel present in the local machine in the following example:
```
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
# Function to be parallelized

919

In this case, greater efficiency is highlighted when we perform calculations using Joblib.
However, we will have to clarify something while dealing with NumPy. This library
has internal vectorization systems that, if used, will lead to greater efficiency compared to
Joblib, since it also bypasses the operation of Python. In fact, NumPy is designed to exploit
low-level optimizations, by using libraries such as:

• Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS)

## • LAPACK

• Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD)

```
These libraries perform operations directly at the CPU level, while taking advantage of
```

the instructions optimized for numerical calculations. When normalizing an array with
NumPy, the entire operation occurs in memory and on blocks of data, without the overhead
of Python loops. Let us see, for example, how to use vectorization in the previous case.
```
mean = np.mean(large_array)
std = np.std(large_array)
start_time = time.time()
results = (large_array[:1000] - mean) / std
